speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill for the second reading of Bill No. C-49 to provide for the establishment of a national energy board.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned last evening I was making the point that we had done very little to solve one of the problems outlined by the Borden commission, that of the financial manipulation that takes place from time to time, an outstanding example of which was that which occurred with respect to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. I pointed out that an official of that organization having made an investment of approximately $8 received a return of something over $1 million. The commission pointed out that investors are entitled to receive a fair return on their equity, but I suggest that even the government would agree that a return of this size in relation to the total investment is unreasonable.
We in this group are interested in the energy bill. Energy affects all Canadian people. This is a matter of interest not only to hon. members from western constituencies, nor is this a bill just to regulate or decide on the price of gas. Natural energy concerns everyone. Our heating, cooking and home illumination are provided by natural forms of energy, and all these aspects of the question should be considered in relation to this bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I feel I should ask the house to settle itself and hon. members who have business to transact in the house to do it in such a way that it will not make it impossible to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in northern Ontario are vitally concerned with this bill. In the days of the founding of northern Ontario the potential of the natural resources there was well known to the traders and trappers who passed through the area over a period of years. Of particular interest at that time was the potential lumbering industry. When the development of that part of the country took place other forms of natural resources were found. In northern Ontario communities have been built around two major industries, the lumbering industry and mining which includes nickel, cobalt, silver, gold and copper. These industries have built many of the towns in northern Ontario,

and these communities are totally dependent on these industries. Communities such as Timmins, Kapuskasing, Kirkland Lake, Ma-tachewan and Cobalt, which have all the facilities of modern towns including housing and schools and which should be capable of supporting a large population, have been unable to expand or even maintain a normal rate of growth.
It was thought that one stimulating factor would be the advent of gas. What happened when this new and potent form of energy was introduced in northern Ontario? A pipe line was built through our part of the country. A number of people who might be called land agents of the pipe line company came in to get easements of land for the construction of the pipe line.
The bill refers to expropriation. This was not a promise in northern Ontario; it was a threat. Many of the people had their arms severely twisted by the threat of expropriation. They were told that if they did not give easements to the company they would be taken to court where they would have to go through the process of law, and would have to give up rights pertaining to their farms whether the line happened to be going through the barn or the house or some other place. They were told that they were going to have to give these easements for a lot less than the company was offering.
I would suggest that the bill has all the inherent faults and problems that we were faced with, because the expropriation section is based on the old Railway Act and, as everyone knows, you can expropriate the land to build a railway from coast to coast much more easily and cheaply than you can expropriate a piece of property 66 feet wide on a man's farm. It would take several years to go through the due process of law, and the farmer would have no farm left by the time he had fought the case through the many stages necessary to conduct his case.
We have not given consideration in the bill to the people who are affected with respect to easements, but we have given a great deal of consideration, as we always do, to the people who are going to make fortunes as a result of the bill. They are going to have the law on their side, as has always been the case. There is going to be justice for the rich and no justice for the poor. I know many farmers in my area who did not get a fair deal even after we made a very strong case publicly on their behalf. The amounts were tripled and raised even higher in many cases, but they still did not get a fair and reasonable deal.
The transporting of energy through a pipe line was looked forward to in northern Ontario as something that would solve some of
National Energy Board the problems with which we are faced. Most of our industries are based on natural resources that cannot be renewed, and the ones that can be renewed have not been or it does not appear that they are going to be. I speak of the forest industry. As far as the mining industry is concerned, the towns involved are withering away through lack of impetus to bring about further development in the area.
Gas coming into northern Ontario could mean a great number of things. It could have meant the development of a low grade coal project we have in the area. If this energy could have been supplied at cost it could have made possible the development of this low grade coal deposit. We also know that in the wastes which come from our mines in the form of slag we have a great potential so far as building materials are concerned. If we were able to use this energy for the betterment of that part of the country we probably could develop a process to transform the slag into building blocks in one form or another, and thus utilize many of the wasted assets connected with the mining industry.
We have depended on hydro power, we have depended on coal and oil. Each of these commodities is terrifically expensive, and that is not because of the geographical position of that part of the country. We made arrangements many years ago to sell hydro power to southern Ontario. We made arrangements to sell timber to other parts of the country. As to the gold, coal and nickel industries, they are not designed so they can be advantageous to our secondary industries. Oil costs us 29 cents a gallon, and the price is not competitive with that of oil in other parts of the province.
We have raw materials available in the form of wood and many minerals. All we need is a source of energy which will allow us to process them into completed products and thus be the basis of our secondary industry. But when gas came into northern Ontario it did not supply this need. Therefore we are suggesting that again the Canadian people have not been given the things they expect from our natural resources. They have not worked to our advantage.
We say this bill is just a cover-up for a lot of mistakes in many other bills. It is a conglomeration of a number of other bills, and it does not set up a new national energy policy. One of the Conservative members rose last night and said that eastern members should help to pass the bill immediately because it only affects the people of the west. That is not what we want from a national energy bill, and that is not what we are going to support.

National Energy Board
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher):
That this bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
In moving this amendment, Mr. Speaker, I am doing what the Leader of the Opposition said he wished to do. I have also decided on the committee to which the bill should be sent, something on which he could not decide, and we hope we will have the support of the opposition in our effort to refer this matter to the committee for further consideration.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to express my regret that by reason of circumstances I could not control I was not able to be in the house last evening when the Leader of the Opposition spoke on the bill, for after all I was most anxious to hear his views on this very important measure. While one can read Hansard, it never conveys the message to the same extent as listening to the spoken word. As I proceed I shall be making mention of some of his suggestions and some of his references.
However, I must say I am glad that the opposition has seen fit, as I apprehended his remarks, to support this measure which is so necessary to the development of our country. I shall also refer to the amendment just moved by the C.C.F. party which, of course, as I understood from an earlier speaker, builds its case on a policy of national ownership of those things that are required for national development.
I shall commence simply by speaking of the purposes of the bill, and I think the explanatory note sets forth those purposes, "to assure to the people of Canada the best use of energy resources in this country." In other words this is another step forward in the national economic policy of the government wherein positive action is being taken. Indeed, there is no other basis for national development than through the medium of such a policy in which the state provides the climate and the opportunity for development while at the same time maintaining the public interest and denying injustice in the carrying out of development plans by private industry.
I remember so well, and I speak now for the moment in so far as the C.C.F. amendment is concerned, that prior to 1944 the solution for every problem in Saskatchewan connected with the development of that province depended on nationalization and control by the state. I find, however, that in the light of the experience those in the government of that province have gained, they no longer have that same feeling of

massive adherence to the doctrine of socialism which they had prior to taking office.
I am one of those who are opposed to anything in the nature of unjustified or inordinate profits made without risk. The essence of profit is the foundation upon which jobs are assured. You cannot expand a nation unless there is a reasonable and proper return, that return being dependent, in size in particular, upon the degree of risk undertaken by those who are prepared to invest their money in these plans. The hon. member for Timmins said he had read the Borden commission report and it seemed to come close to recommending public ownership. I have read that report from end to end, but I see nothing to indicate support for that contention.
I think I should mention the transition, the metamorphosis that has taken place in Saskatchewan, when these hon. gentlemen opposite speak with horror of fair returns to industry. A moment ago there was a speech, and it was similar to one that was made a day or so ago, regarding the awfulness of expropriation. Well, we have expropriation in our province and we also have the means by which the individual may assure himself, through the courts, about the way in which it can be done and those circumstances have been disclosed.
When these hon. gentlemen speak in lachrymose words and tones regarding profits, non-risk and the like, I would remind them of one or two recent examples in Saskatchewan wherein the government of that province has seen fit not to maintain the principle of public ownership but indeed to invite private enterprise into Saskatchewan fortified by the guarantee of the provincial government. I am not going into the particulars in this regard unless hon. gentlemen have a curiosity for full information. However, I would remind them of one or two recent examples. One of the latest examples is the establishment of a steel mill in Regina. In that case the government of Saskatchewan backed the loan to the extent of $10 million, according to the Financial Post, and there were 2 million common shares authorized. Of those, 130,000 were offered to the promoters at 60 cents a share.
Banish the thought, Mr. Speaker, of the government of Saskatchewan agreeing to guarantee and back private enterprise companies which were not undertaking too great a risk, but in this instance they allowed the promoters to take 130,000 shares at 60 cents a share. Do you know why they did so, Mr. Speaker? I do not, but it is interesting to note that the provincial treasury took 180,000 shares at the same rate and the

sponsoring group took a further portion of those shares at $5.40. Finally, there was a public offering to the average person at $6 per share.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Now, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) may believe that this is different from oil companies. Well, as the result of a guarantee by the provincial government this company, and indeed another company, a cement company, as well as the Prairie Pipe Company, were able to go into Saskatchewan and establish themselves under a guarantee of their bonds by the government of that province, in whole or in part, and for that 60-cent investment, in which there was no particular risk, the promoters and the treasury of Saskatchewan could, if they were to take the price of the shares set in a public offering, get $6. I am not going into further particulars about these companies unless anyone exhibits a zest for further information in that regard.
Is it not strange, Mr. Speaker, that they are still speaking of the merits of public ownership? I ask these hon. gentlemen to go out to Saskatchewan to see the experiment in operation. They went to New York to get financing; they found it necessary to go to private enterprise when Alberta and Manitoba were advancing very rapidly in the matter of resource development, with a view to seeing whether or not it would be possible to secure the necessary funds so that Saskatchewan, which was presumed to be the experiment in nationalization and socialization, would be able to catch up with the other two provinces. It is well to keep these things in proportion, and it is well to realize that when these facts were pointed out to the hon. member for Assiniboia he answered in words to this effect, "Well, it is different". Perhaps I should read from the article in question. It is an article dated December 1, 1958 in the Globe and Mail, and reads:
Speaking recently in Vancouver, Mr. Argue said parliament should pass a law making it illegal for company promoters to offer stock to the public at more than they themselves paid for it, or conversely, that they should not be permitted to get it for less than the offering price.
Then it goes on to say:
In Saskatchewan in the last three years three industries have been launched with government financial assistance. In each instance promoters obtained stock below the price asked the public. In the latest venture-Interprovincial Steel-the C.C.F. government itself owns the biggest block of promotion stock.
When this was brought to the attention of the hon. gentleman he said, "Well, these are different types of companies". These vocal rules he had established became obliterated in the light of experience. I point these things
National Energy Board out by way of introduction because the hon. gentleman said this, as reported on December 27 in the Regina Leader-Post:
-his criticism of shares being given to individuals at low cost, was confined at criticism to pipe line companies.
I will allow him to extricate himself from his own reasoning in due course.
The latest thing is the motion that this matter should be submitted to a committee. Throughout this session I have heard complaints that so many committees have been set up that it is impossible for hon. members to discharge their responsibilities. Here we have legislation for which the government must take the responsibility. Royal commissions do not legislate. They hear the evidence; they make recommendations, and governments act on the basis of accepting those portions which in the opinion of the government will meet the exigencies of the moment. We have had two commissions on this matter. The official opposition say the Gordon commission covered this situation. The Gordon commission sat for a long while. It sat for $1,380,000 worth of time. It was covering the history of Canada for the next 25 years and, as an incidental in the recommendations it made, it dealt in part with this question.
As I remember the facts in connection with that commission, the report in general was available in September of 1956 although it did not officially come into the possession of the government until December 6 of that year. The Leader of the Opposition says, "We are all for an energy board; we came to that conclusion in January, 1958". The Gordon commission recommended the setting up of such a board in December of 1956. I brought the matter before the House of Commons in February, 1957 and I remember the disparaging answer given by the then minister of northern affairs and national resources to the effect that all was well- and a reading of his speech at that time will indicate support for my contention thereon -that there was no need for such a board.
While the recommendation was made by the Gordon commission, it was not acted upon. The former government was in power until June 20. The house sat until April of that year, yet no action was taken. It was not until January, 1958, according to the Leader of the Opposition, that the Liberal party Anally came to the conclusion that this particular recommendation was in accordance with its wishes, its desires and its hopes.
I would say this. I intend to review the bill in general without referring to the sections, something of the nature of the bill

National Energy Board that is before us and its reasoning. A moment ago I said it marks a further major step in the implementation of a great national development policy for which this government received a mandate from the people of Canada. A national energy board covers this particular phase of the entire situation, namely energy within the definitions contained in paragraph 2. The Leader of the Opposition says there should be a national energy policy in a statute. I do not know what kind of a statute it would be if it were to contain generalities with respect to national development. This is but another step in that national development policy.
As to coal, and in particular maritime coal, this government has taken forward and important action in order to assist the miners of the maritimes. Tomorrow, I will be in western Canada, in the province of Saskatchewan, to see taken one further step in that national development plan, namely the beginning of the work on the South Saskatchewan dam. For many years members in various parts of the house asked that action be taken in this regard and pointed out the possibility that the time would come again-as has happened recurrently in the last 100 years- when drought and the like would overwhelm those particular portions within the Palliser triangle. This year conditions are not as hopeful as I should like them to be.
Over the years, over and over again, there have been advocates in support of this tremendous undertaking. We received promises, qualified and unqualified, from 1949 on; but it was only when this government came into power that action was taken in this regard and a beginning was made on this project.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister is now giving us a dissertation on irrigation in western Canada. In it he might include the request for deficiency payments made this morning by the farmers of Canada. What have these matters to do with the bill now under discussion? In the last few days, Mr. Speaker, we have been held strictly to account. You have ruled us out of order on matters which had more relevancy than this. I would ask you to remind the Prime Minister that he is not immune from the rules of this house any more than any other hon. member.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not know whether or not the Prime Minister wants to reply before I say anything on this subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with becoming modesty in so far as this government is concerned I was trying to answer the Leader of the Opposition, who said last night that

this bill did not go far enough and that it should go further. I am showing that it is just a step in the national development policy. That causes the hon. member for Essex East, by reason of his own conscience bothering him, to be just a little bit exasperated.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. You will recall that yesterday you ruled an amendment out of order because it dealt with public ownership, a subject which you considered to be irrelevant to this bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am not sure that the Prime Minister was talking about public ownership.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: He was.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: As I understood the point of order, it was concerned with the South Saskatchewan dam, which is somewhat remote from the problem we have in hand, except in so far as it may generate electricity. I am sure the Prime Minister does not intend to stay in Saskatchewan too long. To deal with what the Leader of the Opposition said, it is true that this is not a debate on public ownership, as I have already ruled. I noticed that the Prime Minister got rather far in that field today, but it was in response to what had been said earlier and I do not intend to try to confine the matter too rigidly. But on the point that has been taken I agree that the South Saskatchewan dam is not relevant to this bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: All right, Mr. Speaker; I was trying to give hon. gentlemen some information on this matter. I knew it would be a bed on which they would not want to lie.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Follow the rules.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not want to continue to cause them so much personal suffering.
At that point, Your Honour, I was about to deal with other examples of this national policy, but I shall not do so in view of your ruling. I think, however, I should say something about our energy reserves, not in detail in any way but simply to indicate the importance of this bill, because the attitude taken by the Liberal party is a most unusual one. They support it in principle.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: In principle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
They are opposed to this provision and that provision. They are shocked by certain items. They are annoyed by items which do not exist at all, and they are exasperated by the fact that we are proceeding to do that which should have been done, as they now concede, years ago.
Few countries in the world are so richly endowed with potential sources of energy as

Canada. The hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for Bow River and other hon. gentlemen have over the past months told us something of these vast resources. I am now restricting myself to oil and gas, which provide the opportunity for Canada to stand on the threshold of a new era. The mobilization of these resources of oil and natural gas, coal and hydro power must be assured to guarantee to Canadians the fullest advantage of this land and their heritage.
I shall not deal with the hydroelectric potential or with the tremendous possibilities of the Hamilton river in Labrador, other potentialities on the Yukon river when diverted through huge tunnels into the Taku river, and the undeveloped power in this country amounting to more than 54 million kilowatts. All these are resources that we believe must be developed. Their development must be encouraged now, while at the same time protecting and preserving the public interest. In the western Canada sedimentary basin there are today proven and potential resources which may give to this country the largest crude oil resources in the world. No one can say today what is the possibility and the extent of the black gold which lie beneath the surface in Canada.
It was because of the importance of this matter that we advocated on many occasions a national policy in respect of the various kinds of energy and also the various types of potential development. No one can give any estimate as to how much our oil resources are worth. There are those, however, who have recently estimated that the crude oil resources of Canada are worth $96 billion. In so far as the gas resources are concerned, it is estimated they are worth $40 billion. These are figures which actually stagger but at the same time challenge the imagination of this country.
It was because of this that we endeavoured, not only in 1957 but earlier, to secure some action on the part of the former government. As the then leader of the opposition I set forth our views in this house on February 11, 1957 as reported on page 1160 of Hansard of that date, and on that occasion moved this amendment:
-this house is of the opinion that the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now of a national development policy which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada, encourage more processing of those resources in Canada, correct the present serious unfavourable trade balances, foster wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources, and promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population.
National Energy Board
The answer given at that time, in general, was that no such policy was needed, that we had the necessary legislative powers under existent statutes. I would like to point out before I proceed to deal with the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition just what that legislation comprised. It consisted of an act to regulate the exportation of power and fluids and importation of gas. Fluids are defined as "gas, oil, water or any other fluids, whether liquid or gaseous, that originate or are produced or recovered in Canada". I would point out that that act was passed in 1955 and included oil.
The manner in which the act dealt with licences permitted those things which took place in the Trans-Canada pipe line organization that we, by this legislation, intend to ensure shall not take place in the future. The provision as to licences was under section 3, which reads:
Subject to the regulations and to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve . . . licences may be granted for
(a)	the exportation of power and fluids;
(b)	the importation of gas; and
(c)	the construction or placing of any line of wire-
And so on. Then subsection 2 reads:
A licence to export power or fluids may provide that the quantity of power or fluid to be exported shall be limited to the surplus remaining after due allowance has been made for distribution to customers for use in Canada during the period of the licence.
Then section 6, subsection 1, reads:
No person shall export any power or fluids-
"Fluids" include oil.
-or import any gas except under the authority of and in accordance with a licence granted under this act.
All the powers as they were exercised then were within the limitations which are now objected to by the official opposition. In so far as exports were concerned, regulations were made in this regard. Section 9 of the regulations passed by order in council on June 20, 1955 reads as follows:
The price charged by a licensee for power or gas exported by him shall not be lower than the price at which power or gas, respectively, is supplied by him or his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumption in Canada.
Now, sir, that did not protect Canadians from being placed in the position of subsidizing the cost of gas and the like for another country. That was one of the most serious shortcomings of this legislation as it existed subject to the regulations in 1955, that it was ineffectual in that regard. I remember the momentous debates of three years ago in which we endeavoured to point out to this house and to the country the serious situation

National Energy Board whereby Canadians would pay more for gas in Canada than would the recipients of the gas in the United States after export. In other words, our contention was that action had to be taken in this regard to protect Canadians, both producers and consumers.
The Leader of the Opposition in his remarks last evening seemed to leave the impression, or endeavoured to do so, that the Borden commission had been an expedient, a delaying action. He suggested that the legislation now before us did not clarify the national energy policy, that it left unresolved numerous duplications in function; and in sharp words he spoke of the oncoming dangers of arbitrary government by order in council.
Then he ended by saying, "Let us have a committee on this. The Borden commission made the situation clear and heard evidence over a very considerable period of time, but let us now disregard the evidence which was taken in the past and have this matter submitted to a committee of parliament". I say there is no expedition in that course nor any value in it, having regard to the fullest possible investigation which has been made by these two commissions.
The Leader of the Opposition complained that we had delayed bringing this particular piece of legislation before parliament. I would point out that the time of parliament has been taken up mainly, with the exception of certain items of legislation which have been brought before it, with the debates on the speech from the throne and, latterly, on the budget, and the budget resolutions. The resolution preceding this measure was placed on the order paper early in the month of April. Every opportunity was given for the study of these two reports in the intervening period.
The Leader of the Opposition says that in June, 1958-and I take it that was in a spirit of resignation-the Liberal party came out in favour of an energy commission. Well, I can understand the hon. gentleman's feelings in that regard, for he spoke in the city of Victoria during the election campaign and he dealt with this question. At a press conference he said he would agree to the export of natural gas to the United States.
He took a long time to come to that conclusion-until 1953 or 1954. But listen to these words, the significance of which can only come to the minds of those who were here three years ago.
He said this, but he emphasized-and I can see him as he did so-that this would not be a one-man decision. Whom did he have in mind? Did he have one in mind who is no longer here and who was able to advise the Trans-Canada pipe line company that export


would be allowed in the event that the federal commission in the United States agreed? No longer was there to be a one-man decision.
That is the reason for this type of legislation-to assure that decision will be made by a board; not by such a board as was suggested by one member and reiterated by another, but by a board which, when set up, will hold office during good behaviour for a period of seven years and which can only be removed by the governor in council upon an address by the House of Commons and the Senate. There is not much of the stooge about a board whose members will be placed in the same position as the civil service commissioners, who can not be removed except by a vote of parliament. In other words, to make sure that this board will operate for the benefit of all Canadians it will operate beyond any suggestion of control in any way.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Eyewash. All the powers are subject to the cabinet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
When it comes to eyewash I do not want to compete with the hon. gentleman.
The Leader of the Opposition said he intended to support the legislation. We are glad to see the opposition taking that view. We are dealing with legislation which is difficult to draft-difficult to assure and preserve the rights of Canadians as a whole-and we hope there will be full examination; we hope the views of hon. members of this house with regard to this measure will be placed before the government of the day through the medium of debate.
The board has no power to do other than handle the energy resources of Canada. Mention was made of power exercised by order in council. Let me say that in so far as our great resources are concerned no responsible government would dare place itself in the position where any determination would be made on questions of national policy except on the basis of our legislative system, whereby responsibility rests on the executive with the assistance and the support of the House of Commons and the Senate.
There seems to be general support for the legislation. The broad powers are made flexible enough to assure that risk capital will not be prevented from coming into Canada; it will be invested here, and development will be maintained. I cannot refer to the several clauses, and I do not intend to do so except in so far as I may paraphrase them.
I mentioned a moment ago how entirely free from outside control the board will be. Now with regard to the issue of certificates -and again I am just paraphrasing-someone

has said-and I think I heard the Leader of the Opposition say this-that there would be no assurance that Canadians would have any participation, and that we had strongly advocated the necessity of our natural resources not being owned to an overwhelming extent outside Canada.
I would point out that in granting licences the board has to take several matters into consideration. It is not a perfunctory or routine discharge of responsibilities. The board has to take into consideration the availability of oil or gas or power, the existence of markets, the economic feasibility of a pipe or power line. In addition, it has to ponder another consideration; to deny fly by night promoters, who risk nothing but organization costs, the opportunity to make tremendous profits, inordinate profits. The board must take into consideration the financial responsibility and the financial structure of the company, the method of financing, and-I underline this because it is of material importance-the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line. What could be clearer than that?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if the Prime Minister would permit a question at this point. Is he suggesting that the criteria he has just read from the bill are any different from the criteria which have been applied by the board of transport commissioners for Canada in connection with hearings for leave to construct pipe lines?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not here to discuss what the board of transport commissioners did or did not do, or the criteria they applied. But from now on these criteria, in the event that they are passed by parliament, will be dominant in the determination by the board to give regard to the necessity of Canadian participation.
Finally, even when all these things are determined, a major matter is the question of the public interest which must at all times be one of the considerations in the determination of a recommendation for the issue of a licence. Also, the board can issue a certificate; but it has already received instructions under an earlier clause that it must take into consideration and may add such items and conditions in the issue of the licence as to construction, ownership and operation of the line as it considers desirable or necessary. That is an answer to all these querulous arguments that we have in any way abdicated from the position we took when we determined on the necessity of Canadian participation.
Those clauses of themselves indicate something of the circumstances which must be
National Energy Board taken into consideration and which do in fact protect the public interest. Then, too, there will be no more hiding on the hearings. The hearings will be in public so that all who want to may be present and every opportunity will be given for the fullest possible airing of all the circumstances connected with the matter.
Finally there is the question of whether the public interest will be protected. One of the matters that was the cause of infinite unfairness to Canadians under some of the licences granted when the former government was in power was that Canadians paid through the nose for consumption in Canada while the price in the United States was lower. Members of the former administration said, "We cannot protect you because the regulations say that regard must be had to similar conditions and similar quantities before determination in this regard can be made".
These are a few of the material matters with which this legislation is concerned. Somebody said that the powers should be spelled out. In reply I affirm that they are spelled out and are sufficiently flexible to assure, through public hearings and through maintaining the inviolability of the board by its appointment for a period of seven years unremovable except by vote of parliament, that the public interest can be and will be maintained.
When it comes to the question of appointments we intend to make the best appointments it is possible for us to make.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: All Conservatives.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I did not have the hon. gentleman who interrupts in mind. We intend to assure that those who are on this board will be the best men procurable regardless of any other consideration.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That would be something new in appointments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend must be thinking of the experience in Saskatchewan. We want to assure that the best possible men will be obtained. I know the Leader of the Opposition will agree with me when I say that no one can understate the difficulty of getting the number one, the most outstanding men for these various positions, because of the sacrifice that results from the salaries that are granted. There is no doubt about this, as anyone occupying a position of responsibility will corroborate.
I know this has been my own experience. I have seen outstanding men approached concerning appointments of this nature. They have begun by pointing out to me that in private life they make a great deal more

National Energy Board money and that these are their earning years. They finally conclude by saying that much as they would like to serve the public interest they find themselves unable to sacrifice to that extent.
This is an aside, but may I say that when I was in Australia and New Zealand a few months ago I met a number of outstanding men in the public service there. These were civil servants like those we have in Canada, who make an outstanding contribution. I am thinking out loud now, but I have often personally wondered why they remain in the civil service at the salaries they receive. In speaking to these men of tremendous capacities and great abilities who were prepared to accept salaries far below what they could secure in private life I said, "How is it?" "Well," they said, "we have little rewards that go farther than money can possibly go in compensating us. When we give years of devoted service we ultimately may receive something not in the nature of a title but something in the nature of a decoration which will indicate the state's appreciation for the services rendered."
Mr. Speaker, we experience difficulty in securing the best, but we intend to do everything possible to assure that this board, with the great responsibilities it has to protect the public interest and to maintain the assurance of resource development, will be composed of the most outstanding men who are available; because among other things this board will have the power to determine just and reasonable tolls-and this is of great importance- and shall always, subject to the exception therein given, be responsible for seeing that they are charged equally to all persons at the same rate. That is one of the most important considerations, the determination of just and reasonable tolls, not tolls that by any stretch of the imagination could permit of exorbitant or extraordinarily great profits without risk being attached; such rates that will assure the return that must always be accorded to those who risk, and that will assure a fair return to all and at the same time preserve and maintain the public interest.
I found it a little difficult to follow the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. member for Villeneuve, in what I thought was a most thoughtful speech, argued that the Borden commission was not needed because the work had already been done by the Gordon commission. He said that had all been done but of course urged that a standing committee be set up for public hearings. There were those who said they believe today in a national energy board. Again I would point out what the former minister of northern affairs and national re-


sources said with respect to this matter in 1957.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister give the reference to what Mr. Lesage said in 1957, and the date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a matter of fact I can tell the hon. gentleman that it appeared in Hansard following the motion I moved on February 11, 1957. I have in my hand the notes I took at that time. I have not the copy of Hansard here, but the hon. gentleman could look it up.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps, sir, the Prime
Minister would permit one other question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Surely.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Was not Mr. Lesage at
that time referring not to a national energy board but to a national development policy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This was one of the
elements in a national development policy. I will not cross swords with the hon. gentleman on that because we have proven since how necessary a national development policy was and how development can be achieved by proper encouragement on the part of the government.
I am not going to take very much longer. The three most important features of the legislation are, first, maintenance of the public interest; second, the assurance that the wells of risk investment shall not be dried up; the exercise of important advisory functions under which the board will continue to mobilize statistics relative to power, gas, oil and the like and have up to the minute information in the public interest and, finally, the streamlining of the entire procedure.
I want to deal with one other matter, the question that has been raised as to delay. Under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act exports of oil required a licence which in the case of oil pipe lines was granted freely on an annual basis. However, oil, unlike power and gas, moves fairly freely into world trade. There have been those in this country who have felt that some action should be taken in order to assure, in the event that the United States were to maintain its mandatory controls against the importation of Canadian oil, that there would be a market for Canada's oil and that Canada would have to take the necessary measures to open up a market in Montreal. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) says, why have you that power, which he says is only to be exercised under order in council? I cannot read the clause,

sir, but again it is a question of proclamation. Ordinarily certain statutes provide that the entire statute shall come into operation by proclamation of the governor in council. There have been many such statutes throughout the years. This is not order in council government. This is simply a provision that one portion, instead of the entire act, shall come into effect by proclamation.
The Leader of the Opposition says, why is this, what is the reason? I am reminded again of his words in his speech in Edmonton in the month of February, 1958, when he found himself in a most disagreeable position. Nobody knew what the Liberal policy was on this question and he proceeded to enunciate that policy. The wording of the Canadian Press despatch from Edmonton, February 27, is as follows:
Lester B. Pearson has pledged to Canadan oil producers that as prime minister he would turn over the rich Montreal market to them if the United States continued to restrict oil imports from Canada.
I ask him, how was he going to do that? What were his plans? Were these but words? There is only one way in which it could be done economically and that would be to apply import quotas against those companies that today control the market in Montreal to a large extent.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: But not by order in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Which you would do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: -how the unrepentant have become repentant. The hon. gentleman now admits in effect by that interjection that what he had in mind was the imposition of quotas. Well, anybody who advocates that-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime
Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has quite completely misinterpreted me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, I see. All right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: When I interjected "but not by order in council" I meant it would be done by parliamentary approval and not by order in council of the cabinet.

The fact is that in his Edmonton speech the Leader of the Opposition went on to say:
If Washington will not modify its present attitude with respect to importation of Canadian oil-
These were hard words spoken from the heights of Olympus.
-if the American government insists on placing restrictions on such importations and thus damaging and retarding the national development of a vitally important industry in a friendly neighbour country, then we, in Canada, will have to consider necessary steps to move oil from western Canada into the big market centring on Montreal.

speechtext: I say that as a result of our action these controls were removed. We pressed strongly for their removal. They were imposed in July, 1957 and they would have been imposed by the United States administration regardless of what government was in power in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Importation would have been prevented by the United States to the same degree that it was because the plans had already been made. Public reference has been made to that fact. We acted. We pointed out the difficulties and the impossibility of the position of Canada, with its joint defence relationships with the United States when oil, so necessary to our joint defence and to freedom itself, was excluded. We were able to secure removal of the controls. I will give you something of the picture of the initial effect of the action taken by us resulting in our being able to secure that action by the United States. As generally expected, it means an increase in exports of from 15,000 to 25,000 barrels of crude oil per day. That is a most important and valuable concession. I have before me the Daily Oil Bulletin for May 20, 1959 in which is set forth some of the changes that have taken place as a result of the strong action and strong objection this government took against the importation quotas in the United States. In this publication there is the following:
Effective June 1. crude oil and products brought into the United States from country of origin by pipe line, rail or truck are freed from the restrictions imposed by U.S. import quotas . . . Today the first news of direct impact on western Canadian oil producers was released, when refiners submitted nominations to the Alberta oil and gas conservation board for crude to be delivered in June.
The article goes on to set out that in particular the Texas company has nominated for

National Energy Board its first Canadian crude for its plant at Puget Sound. The article states:
Texaco has called for 8,000 barrels daily of pipe line fill for June, which will mean actual deliveries to its refinery will start by July 1. Shell Oil Company, whose Puget Sound refinery dropped Canadian crude for one year, resumed take in May with nomination for 12,000 barrels daily. Shell's nomination has been raised to 15,300 barrels daily for June. General Petroleum's Puget Sound refinery, a consistent user of Canadian crude, has nominated for 27,400 barrels daily in June, up from 15,350 barrels daily in May. Total Puget Sound nominations for June are 50,700 barrels daily, including the pipe line fill, compared to 27,350 barrels daily in May.
For the United States midwest, June nominations for Alberta crude total 13,400 barrels daily, up from
9.300	barrels in May. International Refineries in Minnesota calls for 7,800 barrels daily, up from
7.300	in May. Bay Refining Company in Michigan calls for 4,000 barrels daily in June, after taking 3,000 barrels in April, none in May. International Refineries Incorporated, will receive 1,300 barrels in June compared to its 2,000 barrel take in May. West Branch Refineries, 300 barrels daily in June after taking that amount in April and none in May.
The over-all Alberta nominations total 352,092 barrels daily, an increase of 51,272 barrels daily, or 17 per cent over the May nominations of 300,820 barrels.
Then it goes on to deal still further therewith. In other words, we have, as a result of the strongest protest that could possibly be made under all the circumstances, been able to achieve with the co-operation of the United States the removal of these quotas which did, in fact, play havoc with the oil industry.
Reference was made to the overruling power of the governor in council. How shocked the finer sensibilities of the Leader of the Opposition were when he referred to that. Let me point out the various boards that are in the same position. The most analogous is the board of transport commissioners, to which reference was made a little earlier. The authority granted to the national energy board is in no way unique. Section 53 (1) of the Railway Act respecting the powers of the board of transport commissioners reads as follows:
The governor in council may at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application; and any order that the governor in council may make with respect thereto is binding upon the board and upon all parties.
In other words, so much has been said about so little, and when you consider the similar powers with respect to the board of transport commissioners there is a complete answer to all these wails about the danger in the authority given the governor in council under this legislation.

I want now to go to one other matter which has to do in particular with the province of Alberta. At no time have I, nor shall I, in any way participate in any degree in a provincial election. I think the Prime Minister should follow that course, and my predecessors have done so. However, when there are statements made in that election or prior to that election, and if those statements do not accord with the facts, then they deserve being commented upon. I intend to refer particularly to a statement made by Premier Manning of Alberta in which he says that one facet of the proposed national energy board is a threat to the further development of the oil and natural gas in Alberta. He goes on to say that if the board is set up there will be a delay in deciding on these applications for export which will be detrimental to the province of Alberta. He said that the processing by the new board will mean a delay of at least four or six months, and the delay is costing the province thousands of dollars, but there is an even greater cost in lost development.
I wish to say in regard to that, that his own words, as reported on November 7, 1957, give the reply. Following an interview in Ottawa Premier Manning said that he could foresee no delay if the international interests require early action by the federal government in approving export permits when new markets opened to Canadian industry by such permits are vital to continued development and expansion of the petroleum and natural gas industry and the national economy. Then, he goes on to say that Ottawa is derelict in its responsibilities in not pressing the major integrated oil companies to accept more Canadian crude for refining. In so far as that statement is concerned, I say to him, it is in your own province where these things happen. It is there that the control can be exercised and I suggest to him that the control, if any, that he has in mind lies in that province because the major companies receive their licences from that government and should have determined for them, by him if he so desires, the action which he asks us to take.
I intend to refer to the question of delay because the boot is on the other foot. There has been an effort made to shift the burden of oil and gas surpluses to this government. I want to make this abundantly clear now. As soon as this bill is put through, the applications of Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, Southern Gas Company Limited, and any other application will receive immediate attention by the board which will be set up immediately after the conclusion of this legislation. There is going to be no delay.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: You already have your appointees in mind, I take it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I said, the question of export permits will receive immediate consideration. I am going to go to the record, because it is intensely interesting. The premier says we have delayed. Let me give the picture in so far as these companies are concerned. In so far as Westcoast Transmission Company Limited is concerned, its application for export was made on July 30,
1957.	Hearings were held on December 10 to 13; December 16 and 17, 1957; January 13, 28, March 4 to 7, 1958; and permission was refused on September 15, 1958. The application was amended on December 9, 1958. The hearings on the amended application took place between January 6 and January 20, 1959, and there was no grant by the government of Alberta of the right to export until April 7, 1959. If it took the board in Alberta, including the original application and the amended application, from July 30, 1957 to finality on April 7, 1959, where is there any solid support for the suggestion of delay by this government?
These records tell the story as clearly as it is possible to tell it, and give the answer to the words to which I have referred. The Alberta and Southern Gas Company applied on October 18, 1957 to the gas conservation board. There were hearings on February 11, 1958 and from March 11 until March 31, 1958 and finally it was refused on September 15,
1958.	Then there was an amended application on December 2, 1958. It was heard on January 6 to January 20, 1959 and was not granted until April 7, 1959.
If it took that much consideration, Mr. Speaker, to determine whether the conservation board of Alberta should decide in favour of exports, where is there any basis for the suggestion that a month and one-half or a little over should not have passed by without action on the part of this government? It might be said that the date of application to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) was, in the case of the first company, December 27, 1958 and in the case of the second company, December 23, 1958. That might be another argument that could be used. That is true enough. But the fact remains that as yet no determination made by the national government would in any way hasten the export because action is required on the part of the federal commission in Washington. That action has not yet been determined.
There are other companies in the same position. There is the Canadian-Montana Pipeline Company. There was an application
National Energy Board to the Alberta conservation board on December 2, 1958; sittings from January 6 to January 20, 1959; application granted April 7, 1959. Again we find the same position of affairs. The application to the minister was on December 24, but any determination on our part in that regard would in no way hasten the export without a decision on the part of the federal commission of the United States.
I agree that it is essential that these matters be thoroughly investigated. I am not complaining at all. It is for the government of Alberta to determine the time to be taken. What I am saying is that if the government of Alberta found it necessary to hold the matter up for the length of time it did so, we must certainly be given every opportunity to look fully into the matter in order to determine the course to be taken. A general examination has been made by the department. Again I come back to this point. In so far as those applications are concerned, they will be processed immediately by the board when it is set up. It will be set up immediately. There will be no need to wait for the mobilization of the board. The members of the board, from the evidence taken by the Gordon commission, the evidence taken by the Borden commission and the evidence taken by the conservation board of Alberta, will be in a position, I am sure, to determine fully the entire question.
With regard to export, it is provided that in the granting of export-and again I reiterate this-the quantity of gas does not exceed the surplus remaining after due allowance has been made for the reasonable foreseeable requirements for use in Canada. It is necessary to maintain that surplus for, after all, these resources are not replaceable. Once gone, they are gone forever. The result is that the primary consideration must be the assurance that Canada in the future shall not find itself handcuffed or in a straight-jacket as a result of the failure on the part of those of us here today to realize the necessity for that degree of conservation which will assure to Canadians full development while at the same time maintaining for future generations the necessary supply without which Canada's industrial development will not be attained.
As to 'the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interests. With the implementation of this legislation, no longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their energy than those paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy. That matter is

National Energy Board extremely important. In the trade world in which we are living, with the conflicts that are accelerating from month to month in the communist trade offensive, above everything else it is necessary for us in Canada, if our international trade is to be maintained, to see to it that we shall not be placed in a position where our costs in connection with energy derived from Canada are greater to Canadians than they are to any other nation, however friendly that nation may be.
As I see it, the bill protects not only the industrial future of Canada but the producer and the consumer. It assures a maximum advantage from the available production of Canada of gas and of power, it being available, in so far as gas is concerned, for export when surplus to the needs of the Canadian economy in this and foreseeable generations in order to ensure for Canadians an adequate supply of the natural resource sources which are the heritage of this country, at the same time bringing to Canada the benefits that are confirmed by profitable export of surplus resources.
When we get into committee of the whole, if there are suggestions on those matters that reasonably will assure the achievement of these purposes, I hope they will be made. My attitude on this matter, as it was when I sat in the opposition, will be that what we are trying to do is to preserve the resources of Canada, to maintain the assurance that the resources shall not be uneconomically wasted and to bring about in this country a development by means of which our country may reach the destiny which its resources make possible.
