speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not attempt to follow the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the emotional effusions he has placed before the house this afternoon. I shall, however, try to deal with the subject bearing in mind relevancy and reason. I quite share the view expressed by hon. members who have spoken previously, indeed on all sides of the house, as to the importance of the subject matter. I must say, however, that I regret that the Prime Minister saw fit to take so much of the time of the house in order to deal with his views on certain provincial governments. The Prime Minister, of course, is entirely free to do as he wishes in the provincial elections, as are private citizens outside of the house. But surely the provincial election in Alberta does not have to be fought in the chamber of the House of Commons. The delightful excursion into local politics in Saskatchewan on the subject of public ownership was probably interesting to some. But having regard to Your

Honour's ruling yesterday and the decision given by Your Honour and, as I understand it, adopted by the house, that that was irrelevant to this bill, it therefore was not a subject for discussion here. The Prime Minister saw fit to make this delightful excursion into local politics in Saskatchewan, but however much one may dislike or like, as the case may be, the particular government in that fine province, it surely is not relevant to this particular bill.
While this rather lengthy discourse was going on this afternoon on all kinds of subjects, some relevant and some irrelevant, erecting a smoke screen in front of the real matters confronting us on second reading of this bill, I wondered what the purpose of the Prime Minister was. I still am not wholly clear what it was.	I cannot help
but recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister made reference to the resolution stage and to how long the resolution was on the order paper. I would point out to him, as I had occasion to point out at the resolution stage, that the resolution did not contain the usual information that resolutions preceding the introduction of bills should contain. It left out all the relevant information, and was therefore of no value whatever by way of notice.
Then a rather extraordinary thing happened. The bill became available for public distribution through the distribution office shortly after twelve o'clock on Wednesday. It is true that certain members of the opposition were able to get copies on Tuesday immediately after first reading. The proposition was put forward on Tuesday night that the debate on second reading should be proceeded with on Thursday. That would be about 24 hours after the bill became available for public distribution. That is a most extraordinary procedure with regard to new legislation of this type, which is a bill involving some 100-odd clauses dealing with such an important subject. Then the Prime Minister intervened and had the matter stood over for one other day, and second reading was started on Friday of last week. So two days were allowed to elapse to enable the public to see the bill.
I have been curious about what it is that the government was seeking to hide. Why was it they were so concerned with not permitting members of the public, particularly those in the industry, to have an opportunity to receive copies of the bill and peruse it? It is particularly interesting to note, in view of the fact that for the two whole years since the government assumed

office in June 1957, they have refused to make any statement of policy on this important subject.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: What was the hon. member doing for those two years? Was he asleep?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The chief whip for the government seeks to make a personal reference but I will let it go by. The fact is that the government has refused, and in doing so has done considerable damage to the industry, to make any statement of policy on the subject of energy resources in Canada, particularly with reference to oil and gas and its exportation and importation, as well as other related matters. But it has now become clear, after listening to the Prime Minister, just what the reason was, after such a long delay in dealing with the subject, for the haste to get this bill through. Such is their determination to prevent the public looking at it and prevent their being heard.
In that connection, it is interesting to note also that throughout the time the Prime Minister took in his speech this afternoon he omitted to deal with the request made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) that this bill, when it gets second reading, be referred to a standing committee where witnesses could be heard. He omitted to deal with that altogether. What are we to conclude? We can only conclude, I respectfully suggest, one thing, that after two years of no policy the government has been somewhat humiliated by having to come to the decision that the policies of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe in relation to the commercial aspects of this matter were sound policies, and that the recommendations of the Borden commission, which were so effective a smoke screen during the last election, were of no value at all and not to be used.
It is true that there are two important matters of principle on which new policies are asserted in this bill. One has to do with the advisory functions of the board, and the other has to do with the import of one of our trade commodities, oil. But on those two matters of principle it is interesting to note that while the government brought in a new policy it did not in either case follow the recommendations of the Borden commission.
With respect to that new principle concerning the advisory committee, it is interesting to note that the legislation provides that the board shall study and keep under review matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction in the field of energy. Energy is not defined in the bill before us. This wholly new principle of charging the board with responsibility and instructing it to study and keep those matters under review is 66968-9-256
National Energy Board a complete duplication in so far as the dominion coal board is concerned, the atomic energy control board is concerned, as well as other legislation dealing with fuel is concerned. It is, as I say, a complete duplication. It is not even in a form which is permissive, but it is a requirement that they shall keep it under review. This means, in addition to the waste and inefficiencies of duplication, that the industry will have to duplicate information and so on. In his remarks on second reading the minister seemed to indicate that he did not visualize duplication, yet it is one of the main principles of the bill which he has introduced.
Then there is another interesting matter. The first report of the Borden commission states that the national energy board shall have the authority to study, review, recommend and so on. In other words, the recommendation of the Borden commission in that respect is repudiated. The minister has given no explanation as to why he chooses to repudiate the report of the Borden commission on that point.
I have other matters with which I want to deal in particular. First of all, there is the question of export. I am sorry that the Prime Minister has left the chamber so quickly after speaking this afternoon, although I understand he had to leave and I think he has explained why, but I wanted to say something about his reference to the export provisions now covering oil. My point is this. He omitted to mention that when that legislation was enacted the situation was that we were relatively small producers of oil.
He omitted that altogether, but, more important still, he omitted those parts of the definition contained in the act which are relevant to his argument, that is, that "export" had reference to export through pipe lines only. That is the one subject which he omitted in his argument about export. In addition, of course, the export of oil began in wholly different circumstances before the development of the oil industry; we now have a margin available for export and the problem is one of finding markets. The hon. gentleman spoke about fluids and, of course, he did not read the definition of fluids, either. I regret that the effect of presenting his case in this way was to make his argument on that point of a nature which would be misleading to any person who was not familiar with the legislation on this subject, and I am sure that is not what he intended.
There is another principle in this bill which I find wrong and difficult to accept. It is to be found in clause 87 where the governor in council is, in effect, given power to control the export and import of oil. This provision

National Energy Board is offensive for two reasons. The first is that by the very nature of the operation of the oil business there would be sufficient time for legislation to be enacted by parliament in the event of any of the difficulties arising such as the minister mentioned in his introductory remarks. The hon. minister knows perfectly well that the construction of refineries is only undertaken when supplies of oil are assured. He knows that contracts for the supply of oil either through pipe lines or by other means cannot be entered into on a day to day basis. Thus there is no possibility of any of the evil things which the minister told us might happen at some dim and distant time in the future occurring so suddenly that parliament would have no opportunity to deal with them. I am one who believes that parliament should have the right to deal with matters of this kind, and I am at a complete loss, remembering the argument used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) when they were in opposition, to understand how they could seek the kind of arbitrary power they are now seeking, and let this proposal get past the draft bill stage and be introduced into this house, having regard to all they said against arbitrary power in a situation which was related to a national emergency and to the national defence of this country.
Now the government wishes to take this arbitrary power and apply it to a trade commodity-a very important trade commodity-when there is no case at all to be made out for doing so. As a matter of fact it is interesting to recall the remarks made by the minister when he was dealing with this subject. He seemed to be very sensitive about it, because in introducing this bill on second reading he had this to say as reported at page 3929 of Hansard:
Therefore we feel there is no requirement of national policy to be served at present by licensing exports of oil.
The hon. gentleman dismisses the matter of exports in that way, though there is, perhaps, some argument which could be made for licensing exports in the light of restrictions of imports by the United States. And in the next paragraph, the Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say:
The case with respect to licensing of imports of oil is different and more complicated. X do not propose to argue the case fully today. It would be premature to do so until the second report of the Borden commission in respect of this matter has been received and considered.
For the minister, having said that, to ask the House of Commons to give him the power of regulation is something which, I must confess, I find strange. Surely if there

is no case to make for the possession of this power, and if it is premature to deal with the question, we should not be asked to pass the authority of parliament over to the minister and his colleagues in the cabinet. Surely that is a principle which is quite wrong and I am amazed at the minister putting it forward. In fact, I suppose one could use such words as "effrontery" to describe the conduct of a minister who comes before parliament and says: I do not propose to argue the case fully because it would be premature to do so until the second report of the Borden commission has been received and considered, but despite that I am asking you to give me these powers. That is closure with a savagery we have never seen.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Nonsense. There is no closure in it at all. You were the proponents of closure in 1956, and you suffered for it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister will not argue the case. He does not propose to argue it. He himself says he cannot argue it because the background against which the matter could be discussed is not yet available. Despite this, he says: give me the power. If that is not closure, then nothing is. It prevents any argument on this subject and I respectfully suggest that the question of whether there should be control of oil imports is a very important matter, and that if and when any government decides that controls should be applied, that is a matter which should come before this house for debate and decision. I am still old fashioned enough to consider that there is some virtue in debate in parliament on these matters and that our discussions throw some light on the subject and enable a better decision to be taken.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I wish you had held that view in 1956.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: We wish you held that view today.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: There is a marked difference between what was done in 1956 and what is being done today. In the case which the minister has in mind I would recall for the benefit of hon. members that there was three weeks debate on the legislation in question. This way, the minister is not going to permit any debate at all.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is not true. You can have all the debate you want for as long as you want.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me remind the hon. minister that he has been given a high responsibility of administering and directing the trade policy of this country. That is a very difficult and complicated task and one of great importance to the economy generally.

The hon. gentleman must surely have learned something from that foolish 15 per cent trade diversion policy put forward at one time. Here he is now seeking to put another product that has historically moved rather freely from country to country under the arbitrary control of himself and his colleagues without even a debate on it in parliament. I invite him to consider what he is doing in asking for such authority.
Let me remind the minister of one other thing. The Prime Minister spoke at great length today about making our resources available to the Canadian people which is an excellent sentiment but there is another facet to this matter. The availability of energy is basic to the development of our whole economy, there is no doubt about that at all. Allow me to place on the record a statement made by Mr. John Davis in a booklet entitled "Canadian Energy Policy" published by the Canadian institute of international affairs. At page 6 of the booklet we find these words:
-the basic difference-
Between Canada and the United States.
-is one of price. Even in 1958, consumers in Canada were paying between 30 and 50 per cent more for their energy than were their opposite numbers in the U.S.A.
The point I want to make out of that is that I hope the minister will bear in mind the cost of energy sources to suppliers and producers who are seeking to export. These things should be considered. The Prime Minister chose not to deal with this question in his lengthy remarks this afternoon. I suggest to the minister that he take another look at the principle that he is trying to assert in this bill on this point and that he consider withdrawing it.
May I also point out that this is the type of question on which we could get information if the minister would permit this bill to go to a standing committee where evidence could be obtained on all these points.
There is another thing I want to point out about the minister and his colleagues taking this arbitrary power. This is bad not only on the grounds of it being arbitrary power vested in the minister but it is also bad to provide import control in such a way that the first report of the Borden commission which is outstanding could be incorporated in it. Section 19 of that report which deals thoroughly with the subject provides rather drastic controls. I think the minister will agree with my description of them as being drastic. I commend section 19 to the attention of the minister. With that kind of comprehensive and burdensome control recommended in the report of the Borden commission and with the minister and his colleagues assuming this 66968-9-256J
Interest Act
arbitrary power to deal with this subject, does the minister not see what could happen in places like the maritimes? Is anyone going to develop refineries in the maritimes to supply purely local needs? There are great problems like that which should be debated in this house at a time when the government feels it has any information that would warrant putting on import controls. Does the minister not see the damage that could be done to the development of this industry in assuming this power, damage that would be unnecessary and improper and that would have the effect of sharply increasing the cost of our energy in the meantime?
The Prime Minister this afternoon raised the same old cry about the former government not establishing this board and he referred to the Gordon commission report. The Prime Minister raised this matter in the house on January 15, 1957, when he asked the then minister of trade and commerce if he would agree to the suggestion in that report about setting up a national energy board. Mr. Howe in reply said that he had not considered the matter and that the decision would be one for the government rather than for an individual minister and that he did not want to give his opinion at that time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, February 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Argue for the second reading of Bill No. C-3 to amend the Interest Act and the amendment thereto of Mr. Roberge.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the explanatory note of Bill No. C-3 reads as follows:
Section 2 as at present provides that there is no restriction as to the rate of interest except as provided by statute. The amendment limits the rate to 12 per cent.
This bill was the subject of a full day's debate on February 12 last at the conclusion of which the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) moved an amendment as recorded at page 962 of Hansard in the following words:
That the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

Interest Act
Following the amendment a number of hon. members participated in the debate and spoke in favour of the amendment. I want to go on record as favouring the amendment but I wish to say a few words on the bill itself in order that my expressed reaction will be available when the amendment goes before the standing committee on banking and commerce.
Naturally I am opposed to high interest. High interest in Canada is not justified on any ground. However, when we consider interest I think it is only fair that the word itself should be interpreted in the usual and customary way. Credit must be available to keep our factories in production and to make it possible for Canadians to maintain their high standard of living. Extended credit is necessary for the housing industry, for automobile manufacturers, household appliance firms and every other type of business in Canada. Credit is the backbone of the nation and without it millions of our citizens would immediately be put out of work.
The problem I see in the bill is who should have credit and at what price. We have various types of credit. The first and common type of credit is first mortgages. In my short time as a lawyer I have seen first mortgages bearing interest running from 4J per cent up to 8 per cent and higher. If a maximum rate for any type of interest is to be fixed, let us not do anything that may encourage an increase in the interest rate of first mortgages.
Another common type of credit is bank credit. Credit is given to a customer depending on his credit standing and in many cases with security. I am a bit afraid if we pass the bill in its present form we may be opening the door to encourage the banks to demand an amendment to the Bank Act which will permit bank loans for normal purposes at a higher rate of interest.
I think it is only right that I should refer to the report made by the banking and commerce committee in 1938 so far as the word "interest" is concerned. I refer to page 418 where I find the third report of the standing committee with respect to its inquiry into small loans and small loans companies. At that page the following appears in the report: That the search for a "reasonable" rate of interest should have continued over the ages is largely due to the application of the word "interest" to dissimilar uses.
In the same paragraph the concluding sentence reads as follows:
While under our present economic system we have imperfect competition, it is manifest that given a sum of $100,000 for investment the rates on its return will necessarily differ as to whether the sum is say: (a) invested in a block of Canadian 
government bonds, (b) lent to 50 land owners secured by first mortgages, or (c) distributed in lots of $200 to 500 people of nondescript occupations on personal security.
In explanation the final paragraph on the same page reads in part as follows:
While loans on personal security are made tor diverse purposes, as set out in our records, and contain different degrees ol risk, they possess two common features that affect the element of cost, namely: "size" and "time", i.e., they are small loans made for short terms. Quite obviously the purchase of a block of 12-year Canadian government bonds requires little expenditure for investigation and none for supervision; investments on 50 farm mortgages, for varied periods, entail considerable cost for both investigation and supervision; while the investigation of 1,000 applications to effect loans to 500 people for a few months, with meticulous supervision, becomes expensive business when expressed as a percentage rate of $100 on a monthly basis.
I suggest it is only fair that all of us must remember that recommendation when considering this bill either in this house or before the standing committee. In the previous debate there was serious criticism of Eaton's and Simpsons-Sears. Both of these firms do business in my riding and I feel that the criticism was not entirely justified. The mover of the bill suggested that these companies charged up to 54 per cent on instalment purchases. He explained that on an instalment sale of $20 the customer paid a minimum of $2.25 and that this amounted to 54 per cent provided the loan was paid to the firm at the rate of $5 per month.
I have not made any effort to check the computation but I think when he refers to interest he is overlooking the important factor of other costs. Surely the firm is entitled to make some charge to a willing purchaser for the cost of staff salaries as a result of the office work entailed, bookkeeping expense, the cost of ledgers, the cost of collection and perhaps the cost of loans or financing in order to maintain inventories.

One thing that I believe should be kept in mind is how much of the cost, about which the hon. member has been questioning me, is actually interest. I think the house should be more concerned about making finance houses, small money lenders and instalment vendors show clearly

the annual rate of interest rather than the monthly rate which we see advertised so often in their advertising "come-ons". I believe this rate should not include the costs I have just mentioned and others necessary to record a legal document in a registry office in order to protect the vendor. Another thing which I feel is related to the subject under discussion, and which I believe is in order, is the subject of loss leaders. Personally, I believe they are related to the subject of interest. People under a free enterprise system like to take advantage of a bargain, and in their anxiety to take advantage of a loss leader, which is strictly a gimmick of the retailer-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Order I shall have to ask the hon. member how he would relate loss leaders to an act to amend the Interest Act which is before the house this afternoon.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: The reason I think it is related is that loss leaders tempt people into a store. They sign credit contracts, and when they sign these contracts they are, in some cases, paying exorbitant rates of interest, etc.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Good for you; you have finally come to it, have you?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
They pay exorbitant rates of interest or selling costs which are not all true selling costs. In any case, whatever they pay for, it is related to the subject because the result is to place that many more contracts into existence, and they are reflected in the total millions of dollars of credit extended to the people. This leads people to buy things that they cannot afford, and in many instances the loss leader type of contract is responsible for a man getting himself into debt to 15 or 20 creditors and eventually arriving at the door of the moneylender.
Since the end of the war the government has done a lot to help the home owner. It has done a lot for the farmers and fishermen, and we all hope it will do more. Through the creation of the industrial development bank it has done a lot to help small industry. What has it done to help the automobile industry? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the automobile and truck industries have contributed more to the growth of the small loan companies and the moneylenders of this country than any other commodity. Why could the government not consider the creation of a crown company to make money available at reasonable rates of interest to those people who are employed in the trucking industry? This would make it possible for the small loans companies, the finance
Interest Act
companies and other types of moneylenders to have more money available and if they had an excess of cash I am sure the rate of interest, about which we are concerned, would automatically come down to a more reasonable level.
The high interest rate is the main cause of inflation. This bill itself would not curb it. A few years ago if a man was in debt he might lose his job if his employer found out about it. I have had examples of people having garnishee orders served upon them, and as a result they advised me that if the judgment were not paid in full the employer would not keep them on the payroll. The finance companies have, in this one instance in my opinion, done quite a service to the public in permitting some people to consolidate their debts. This has given these people some peace of mind.
My main criticism of the finance companies is the type of advertising they put out. In today's Globe and Mail there is an ad which I saw at five o'clock. It is in the classified pages and reads:
Second mortgages, $2.49 Interest weekly-
Then the words, "for every thousand dollars you borrow", are in small print. There follows the name of a certain mortgage company in Toronto. If the loan remained in existence for a year, this rate of interest on second mortgages would be in excess of 12 J per cent per thousand dollars, on what might be considered a fairly secured risk in the city of Toronto. If it is necessary to pay up to 12J per cent for some types of second mortgages which are secured debts, how would it be possible for finance companies to make loans at the suggested rate of interest? I believe that these advertisements must be regulated. I do not believe it is proper to advertise "Money for loan" in large black type, and then follow it in small type with the words, so much per week for every thousand dollars borrowed. I believe that the house should consider the necessity for regulating the type of advertising, and I suggest we should seriously consider making it compulsory to advertise an annual rate of interest as opposed to a weekly or monthly rate. In this way it would be possible for the average person to readily compute what he would be paying for the money borrowed, and at the same time make it convenient to compare the rates demanded by various companies.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I believe it only fair that finance companies should be permitted to charge a rate over and above what second mortgages demand, and over and above what the banks request. In my opinion the house should give serious consideration to making it possible for the finance companies and moneylenders to itemize their

Interest Act
costs separate from their interest income. These companies maintain properties, pay office expenses, and a great many people throughout this country are employed by them. I think that the cost of the loan should be itemized separate and apart from simple interest per annum. At the present time the various financial companies, small moneylenders and retail credit vendors, have outstanding nearly $2 billion loaned to the people of Canada. This has done a good deal toward helping provide employment and keeping the industries of the country going.
As I said earlier, I would encourage the house to give serious thought to regulating the loss leader type of merchandising; to give some thought to recommending to the government that truckers, who cannot borrow except through finance companies, be entitled to borrow money, as their fellow Canadians do, from crown corporations at reasonable rates of interest; and that some regulation should be introduced governing the type of down payment that vendors in this country must insist upon. This would discourage people from buying things that they cannot afford. I know that it looks relatively easy to put out a dollar or two dollars a month to buy a certain article or piece of household equipment. However, when you add these payments on to the payments to which people have been previously committed for other types of merchandise, it does not take long before people have become indebted to 15 or 20 creditors, which makes it impossible on pay day to give each and every one of them 50 cents or a dollar.
All of these suggestions which I have mentioned would automatically reduce the volume of business that the moneylenders are doing. As I said before, if their business is reduced, they will have an excess of cash available and money will be lent by them at more reasonable rates.
In conclusion, I wish to put on the record a statement that, in my opinion, the finance companies and the moneylenders of this country have done a service to this country. I refer to an editorial which appeared in The Albertan on Wednesday, April 4, 1956. This editorial is long but I intend to put only a couple of paragraphs on the record. It is entitled "The Small Loans Business" and it reads in part:
The C.C.F. members of parliament have been opposing two private bills having to do with small loans companies. One would give a company already in business a more attractive name, the other would incorporate an American company which happens to have the national president of the Liberal party as one of its dummy directors-
Later on the editorial states as follows:
The Albertan has no sympathy with the practice of levying exorbitant interest. We acknowledge the

seeming injustice of people most desperately in need of money having to pay the highest rates of interest.
With that paragraph I am in complete agreement as, I am sure, are all members of this honourable house. The editorial states further:
Banks and mortgage firms offer money at reasonable rates. If the borrower can't qualify for a loan there, in most cases he could have been an active member of a credit union and borrowed from it. Credit unions more and more are meeting the need for small loans, and still they have a long way to go before they have reached the limit of their possible expansion.
The concluding paragraph of the editorial states as follows:
We doubt that there is any more moral justification for government controls on the price of money than on the price of housing rental, the price of automobiles, or the price of pickles. Anyone who objects to the price someone else is charging is free to offer that commodity at a lower price.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state that this editorial expresses in most certain terms most of my thinking on this important bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house are in sympathy with the intent of this bill. The problem of usury has faced governments and peoples down through all written history. In his introduction to the bill the sponsor of it stated that this bill would control part of the area of small loans. He pointed out that as to small loans companies the ceiling on their loans on which control was exercised had been raised from $500 to $1,500. This was done under the former minister of finance, Hon. Walter Harris.
I spent some time going back and reading some of the statements made during the sittings of that committee. I found many of them to be pertinent to the bill that is now under consideration. It was pointed out that the degree of risk inevitably was reflected in a higher rate of interest; that if a person is not a good credit risk, he pays more for his money. The problem, of course, is how to legislate people into dealing prudently with their resources or how to legislate people into being good financial managers of the resources they may have. I believe that is a problem that would stick even our friends in the C.C.F. group. It comes back to human nature.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) makes a passing reference to this matter as reported at page 949 of Hansard. He states as follows:
Canadians need credit. They have to have credit, and when they have to have credit they are forced to pay these fantastic rates of interest. I am suggesting that the government should take action in this field, and should study this whole question.

With all the good will in the world towards the intent of this bill, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the statement made by the hon. member is certainly open to question. Canadians need credit. Everybody needs credit. Our whole business economy is fashioned and based upon an extensive credit system. But we need credit within the resources which we have and which will allow us to repay the loans we receive. If a person is making $4,000 a year and that is the extent of his resources, I doubt whether that person would be a good credit risk for a loan of $40,000 or $50,000.
I well remember that, in canvassing in the election of June, 1957, I met a lady who said to me, "Why can't you do something about these loan sharks?" She was referring to the way in which the future of borrowers is mortgaged to the point where they have no reserve whatsoever for any eventuality that might come up, where they are prisoners of their own enthusiastic buying. After discussing the matter for a little while, she came to the conclusion that they would work their own way out of it, that they would never get caught again but also that this tale of their experience would not help their neighbours who would have to find out for themselves.
I know of other cases about which I have been told where a cash sale has been refused at the price originally offered because the salesman expected that it would be a time payment matter. It was quite clear that the interest rate would be quite high, and that is where the profit of the sale lay.
The advertising mentioned by the hon. member who spoke previously can be seen when you walk down the streets. It seems to me that the largest customers of the neon companies are the loan companies because, wherever you look you find there is one advertisement after another staring at you. Their advertising is to be found in the busses as well as in the newspapers. But at the same time these people give a useful service in the way of advancing credit which the person receiving that credit could not normally secure.
Credit unions have been mentioned. I helped to found a credit union. Over the years I have periodically had loans from that credit union and I paid 12 per cent interest. It is true that I obtained a rebate but the rebate was not very much. There is little risk to a credit union. They know everybody in it. The greater part of the loans they make are secured. Nevertheless they still are obliged to charge that interest rate in order to break even. This is a nonprofit organization.
Interest Act
We have heard from the superintendent of insurance of the success of the Bank of Nova Scotia small loans plan. I believe the Bank of Nova Scotia was the first chartered bank to go into that field, but even there you pay 12 per cent. I am not arguing that there is no need for control. I would say that the interest rates as set up in the present Small Loans Act are reasonable, because those interest rates reflect the fact that small loans are more expensive to carry and operate than large loans. As the hon. member for Assiniboia undoubtedly knows, on the first $500 the interest rate is 18 per cent, and after that, from $500 to $1,500, it drops to 12 per cent. The intent of this bill would be to raise that ceiling indefinitely, and on that basis the principle is good because the larger the loan the less money it should cost the loan company. However, the only result will be that those loan companies will have become more selective and will have to refuse credit, which perhaps may be a good thing.
I think the hon. member for Assiniboia is certainly not reasonable in his statement which I have referred to, where on one side he says there should be almost unlimited credit, and on the other side he says interest rates should be controlled. Those two things just do not go together. That is another reason why the amendment to send this bill to a committee for further study is a proper amendment. Because a few years back it was wise and right to raise the ceiling to $1,500, perhaps the proper course is not to take the recommendation of the hon. member for Assiniboia in toto but maybe that after study the upper limit should be raised to $2,500 or even $3,500, I do not know. But those facts can be brought out if this bill is referred to a committee to thoroughly investigate the situation.
I do wish to refer to the remarks made by the previous speaker in regard to misleading advertising. I believe that is a subject which has been brought up in the house before and it is pertinent to this particular measure. Misleading advertising in regard to small loans is the sort of thing where you get the small print, where the rate is stated as $10 or $100 and you do not get the rate of interest you are paying per annum, because the original amount of the loan starts to reduce one month later and the interest rate which you may appear to be paying simply does not reflect the true interest rate which in fact you are paying. I think there is room for control there, and I believe further control is needed in the field touched upon in the hon. member's

Interest Act
bill. I do say that in correcting one evil we may jump into or subject ourselves to worse evils.
The whole point, as I suggested at first, is that you cannot legislate people into being good financial managers. If a person wants a loan and there is a law which says he cannot have it, there are always people available to help him break the law by means of turning back a certain amount of the loan and the face value of the loan does not reflect the amount of money he receives, and so on. The fact that the law can be broken is no reason why one should not be there. But whatever law is enacted, it must be enforceable. It must have safeguards in it and it must be reasonable.
I would like to try to find words properly to describe how I feel in regard to the practice of holding people up with fantastic interest rates, and on top of that to make tremendous discounts on the face value of a mortgage. Perhaps a person should not take out a second mortgage, but in many cases people are forced to. They must have a house to live in because they have children and they cannot rent a house. In that last respect if we had more rental accommodation or had some law which compelled landlords to take in families, perhaps matters might improve. Therefore this person is faced with the necessity of acquiring a basic essential of married life, namely a home. If he never makes another mistake in his life, or never has to buy anything else on terms, that one purchase can put him behind for 15, 20, 25 years, because of the bonus which he may have to pay if he has not enough money to make a big enough down payment so that a first mortgage would carry the balance. In that field I have thought that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation might perhaps enter. It may be a field which should be considered entirely separately from the particular point brought out by the member for Assiniboia.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am sure no hon. member wants to see unreasonable interest charges and bonuses imposed on people because they have to have something. We believe that where it is possible the government needs to control the situation. Such a committee I think might well investigate the legislation which other countries have on their books, for example, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States. But in the final analysis, any legislation which is evolved must be legislation which is fair and which is enforceable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill has been before the house a number
of times and we are now debating an amendment that was moved to the bill on February 12. The amendment reads as follows:
That the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.
Although different attitudes are taken from time to time regarding an amendment of that type, it is usually considered that, at least for the time being, it sets aside the bill under discussion and refers not the bill itself but the subject matter thereof to a committee. Mr. Speaker, we have seen a lot of tears- I do not know if they are crocodile tears or not-being shed with regard to the welfare of Canadians who have to pay exorbitant rates of interest. Some members when discussing this bill have complained of the one per cent figure, or the rate of approximately 12 per cent per year. They have said: "Where did you get the figure? Did you pull it out of a hat? Why this figure? Isn't it too low? Won't it cause the companies too much hardship if the rates are reduced to that amount?" Mr. Speaker, I do not think I got the figure out of a hat. It is the rate charged by credit unions in this country, the maximum rate. A great many of them charge less, but as far as I know it is the maximum rate which is charged by credit unions. The credit unions have done a very excellent type of business. They have made a good saving for their customers. They have grown, and I think it is the very maximum rate which should be allowed at this time.
Although the adoption of the amendment before the house would not result in any heady progress with this matter, I do suggest that the very least hon. members opposite should do would be, first of all, to permit a vote on this amendment and, second, to support it. Then they will not be embarrassed, if indeed it is an embarrassment, by having to decide whether or not they think the 12 per cent figure is a correct one. They would be making it possible for the banking and commerce committee of this house to study the question of interest rates and to study the subject matter of the bill, and, I hope, after studying the subject, to take action which would result in the lowering of interest rates.
I have in my hand the Toronto Star for today. I sent for it a short time ago, and I noticed on the front page a heading: "Demand Ottawa Probe 50 per cent Mortgage Bonus". The article reads:
Richmond Hill council last night called for a federal judicial inquiry into the practice of some mortgagors charging up to 50 per cent bonuses for second mortgages in new town subdivision. Coun. James Haggard explained that to get a second

mortgage of $5,000 some homeowners must pay an additional $2,500 as a bonus. This must be paid back with interest.
A resolution calling for the inquiry was passed unanimously. Copies will go to the Ontario minister of planning and development and the Toronto real estate board, council decided.
All Metropolitan Toronto municipalities will be asked to support the Richmond Hill resolution.
The passage of the amendment to this bill will enable this inquiry to proceed immediately in Ottawa before the banking and commerce committee and we could find out whether this nefarious practice, this legal gangsterism which is referred to in this article, should be allowed to continue unchallenged in this country. By talking about this measure and preventing it from coming to a vote, hon. members opposite must accept responsibility for these abhorrent practices being continued. I think it is a disgrace to the free enterprise economy which hon. members opposite champion so strongly that Canadian homeowners should have to pay a bonus on second mortgages reaching the staggering amount of $2,500 on a mortgage of $5,000.
If hon. gentlemen will vote on this amendment, and if the amendment is carried, it will not cause political embarrassment. Surely the whip will not be hard on them; surely the whip will not chastise them; surely, even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will not instigate disciplinary action, because all this would do would be to allow a committee of this house to hear witnesses, take evidence and see whether or not in the opinion of the committee action should be taken in this regard.
I challenge hon. members opposite to quit this farce of talking out this measure time after time, this farce of preventing, by talk, members of this house taking a decision and, by talking out the measure, making it impossible for people in this instance and in many other instances who wish to obtain homes to obtain those homes, and obtain second mortgages, unless they pay staggering and fabulous rates of interest.
The rates of interest charged in this country are not going down. The present government, by its high interest policy, is promoting, aiding and abetting a continuation of this type of gangsterism in the interest field. The government has allowed the rediscount rate to reach the highest interest rate in the history of this country. The tight money policy of the former administration was just a joke compared to the rigid high interest policy of the present administration; apparently there is no limit to be placed upon it. My appeal today is for the government to allow this amendment to go to a vote so that members of parliament may study this question. Then 66968-9-257
Interest Act
let us take action in the interest of the ordinary Canadian to reduce and limit these fantastic interest charges.

I was

speechtext: Better than killing it by talking it out.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
No one has spent more time in talking about bills and talking a lot of nonsense than has the hon. member who sponsors this measure, and I do not think he made any contribution toward furthering the passage of this bill by the remarks he made, if he sincerely intended that it should pass.
I think it is obvious that there is a general feeling in this house that some kind of control of interest rates should be adopted. This bill, when one considers it, is an all-embracing bill in that it defines and covers not only interest as we understand it but all manner of charges including discounts and penalties. I do not think that we can, by a simple formula of specifying a rate per annum based upon the size of a loan, arrive at a figure which would be fair and reasonable and just in all circumstances.
I think that this bill has created a forum for the making of a lot of extravagant and unjustified statements. I have no sympathy with so-called loan sharks, but I do not think it is fair to those who are engaged in the legitimate business of lending money to classify them in a general way of being loan sharks. Neither do I think it is proper for members of this house to rely on newspaper statements and accept those statements as being full statements of all the information on those subjects, and to refer to those involved in terms of gangsterism. I know that in this country we do have elements of gangsterism, but they are certainly not confined to the interest field as the hon. gentleman would have us believe.
This question has two sides like so many other questions and issues that arise from day to day in our daily lives. I think it is generally agreed, as is indicated by the remarks of those who have thus far taken part in this debate, that there is a need for legislation for regulating interest and other charges of a like nature such as commissions, bonuses, investigating charges and perhaps recording and renewal charges, but when you take into account penalties, fines and charges for defaults as is the case in this bill then you are, of course, stepping into a realm of figures just as fantastic as most of the figures we have heard related in this house as being

Interest Act
charges which are unconscionable and unreasonable. Over the years we have accepted penalties as being reasonable but when they are applied and determined on the basis of an annual rate they become unreasonable.
We know, for instance, of utilities that impose a penalty for non-payment of bills which is applied on the first day of the default. It is true that the penalty may be the same whether the default continues for thirty days or even longer but the fact remains that the penalty is imposed on the first day of default. When that is determined as a rate per annum then we enter the realm of percentages ranging from 20 to 50 per cent per annum.
The bill also deals with discounts. Here again we find that premiums are granted for prompt payment. When those are projected into percentages per annum we again find that we reach fantastic rates.
Another objection I have to the bill which I do not believe could be cured by passing the amendment and referring it to the banking and commerce committee is that it is deficient in many respects. I have no doubt that what is in mind in connection with this legislation is the small loan. Of course, we have some legislation in existence dealing with the exacting of interest and maximum rates of interest on small loans. I believe that if we are going to legislate in respect of loans then there should be some limitation in connection with loans on real estate as well. Of course, when we consider that factor we come to the question of security. That again is something not taken into account in the bill now before the house and no attempt is made to spell it out.
Everyone knows that the element of risk has a great deal to do with interest. That may be manifested in many ways but it does obtain very generally in the money market and in the security market.
No one would suggest, for instance, that a loan of a modest amount of money, perhaps to the extent of 25 per cent of the value of a first class real estate property and secured by way of a first mortgage should carry with it a rate as high as if the loan were up to 75 per cent of the value. Instead of criticizing and casting aspersions upon the government of the day in so far as its record in the field of loans is concerned, I think the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) might well have congratulated the government and also might well have mentioned what I consider to be a most significant statement made today concerning the intention of the government to keep the rate on first mortgages down to 6 per cent per annum. That is of much more significance than all our time-consuming debates on small loans.

I know of instances where rates far in excess of 6 per cent are now being exacted on mortgages and I believe the average rate is about 6J per cent. When that is projected over a period of 30 years the borrower really becomes burdened. There is no great burden in his having to pay anywhere from $1 to $5 in interest even though that may represent interest in excess of 12 per cent per annum but when a home owner has to pay an annual rate of interest in excess of 6 per cent which I think should be the maximum rate payable on a home loan and when one considers the length of the term of the mortgage one realizes that it runs into substantial sums of money.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned for private members' hour I was dealing with some of the remarks of the Prime Minister. I had been seeking to deal with his charge that the former government should have provided an energy board and his reference to it being referred to in the Gordon commission report on Canada's economic prospects. I was dealing with his having asked the then minister of trade and commerce on January 15, 1957 whether he was going to set up a national energy authority and his statement that the minister had replied that he had not considered the matter, that the decision would be a matter for the government and he did not care to express an opinion then. It was at that point in my remarks that the interruption in this debate occurred.
I want to continue my argument by pointing out that the Gordon preliminary report had been tabled on January 10, 1957, some five days earlier. It had been made available to the government either in December of 1956 or early January of 1957. Therefore up to that time there had been no opportunity to consider the matter at all. I also

want to point out that the report made reference to a special study being carried out with regard to Canada's energy prospects. That study bears date of March, 1957, and was tabled in the house on November 22, 1957, after the change of government. That report would presumably be a basic document in considering the Gordon report recommendations on this subject. Therefore, bearing in mind that parliament was dissolved on April 12, 1957, it was wholly misleading to the house to suggest that there was an opportunity for the previous government to consider the Gordon commission report on the subject of energy and to deal with it.
Reference was also made to Mr. Lesage, then minister of northern affairs and national resources, and it was asserted that he had been opposed to the setting up of such an authority. In that regard reference was made to a debate but the Prime Minister gave no page reference to Hansard for the then minister's speech. We were left without being able to identify the exact page when the Prime Minister made the assertion. It now turns out that the matter under discussion on that occasion was the whole subject of the treatment of national resources and it was not related to the subject of a national energy authority at all. Nowhere can I find any statement by Mr. Lesage which would indicate opposition to a national energy authority being set up.
Then there was another part of the remarks of the Prime Minister to which I think some reference should be made. I refer to his reading of the criteria set out in the bill for deciding whether or not a licence or certificate should be granted. Perhaps I can deal with that point very quickly. He might just as well have read the criteria from notes he might have got from the board of transport commissioners as to the procedure to be followed in dealing with pipe line applications under the old legislation. They are all there. There is nothing new or changed in the bill in that respect although there is one change in the bill in that it omits certain former legislation that had to do with the price of gas exported from Canada being not less than the price of gas sold in Canada.
Another argument made by the Prime Minister was rather interesting. He took great credit for obtaining the removal of the mandatory controls or quotas applied by the United States against the export by Canada of oil to that country. He is not modest in taking credit for some of these things but there are those who think that maybe his policy involving the famous 15 per cent trade diversion had something to do with causing such mandatory controls to be imposed in the first place.

National Energy Board In any event, granting him credit for having such influence with the United States government as to have that government remove these quota controls, I think his attention ought to be drawn to an article in the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday, May 26, 1959. That article is headed, "Crude Oil Exemption Political Convenience". Perhaps I should read part of the article. I should like to read it all but time does not permit me to do so. It reads in part as follows:
The possibility of any substantial increase in American imports of Canadian crude seems more remote than ever, despite the exemption of Canadian crude from import quotas and the encouraging 20,000 to 30,000 barrels daily increase scheduled for Puget Sound refineries.
The reason for this gloomy assessment is found in section 2, paragraph (c) (11) of the presidential proclamation exempting Canadian oil from the quota. The substance of the paragraph is that the quotas will be re-established if Canadian oil begins to flow in large volume.
It looks as if all the United States has done is to remove a political source of irritation without forfeiting the economic advantages to its producers of the quotas.
Canadian oil, it should be remembered, seldom, if ever, was imported into the United States to the full extent permitted by the quotas. The recession was most often cited in explanation for this. It is now quite apparent other considerations were at work.
The most obvious of these has been the pressure upon American-based international oil companies to keep facilities, refineries, pipe lines and tankers designed for off-shore oil running at maximum capacity.
The initial imposition of quotas was followed by elaborate swap-out arrangements between these companies and between them and American independent producers and refiners, all directed towards concentrating import volume where it would yield the most profitable return.
Canadian oil, while cheaper than American oil in some border markets and in the American northwest, had small attraction to American refiners in these circumstances. The subsequent exemption of Canadian oil has made little difference.
There is a lot more to the editorial but the point I want to make is that the Prime Minister's remarks on that aspect of the subject were something less than complete and put a better picture on the position of Canadian exporters than the facts warrant at the present time. National Energy Board that Canadian industries will be asked to pay a higher price for their energy than that paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy. At that point in his remarks he was referring to gas. I want to point out just how loose that statement is.
How is he going to control the price that foreign industries have to pay for the natural gas they import from Canada? A large public utility in the United States, using vast quantities of gas from a number of sources, may very properly and very probably be taking a small percentage of its total quantity from Canadian sources, and the Canadian government has no control over the retail price charged by this company to its consumers, especially if the bulk of its supplies come from sources within the United States at a lower cost because of proximity or other reasons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take a great deal of the time of the house in adding to the many remarks and observations which have been made during this debate and which I think we will all agree have been, for the most part, of a constructive nature. I have had occasion to express my views before in relation to the problems of import and export, so there is no need to repeat them except as they apply directly to this bill.
It has occurred to me though, Mr. Speaker, in listening to the discussion thus far that we have reached a point in the motion for second reading of the bill presented to us where those of us sitting in our seats in the house or people sitting in the galleries might find it confusing to try to ascertain exactly what we are endeavouring to determine in so far as the objectives of an energy bill are concerned. I fully recognize that I am not the last speaker, nor am I setting myself up as an authority to determine how to summarize the debate thus far. It would, of course, be suggested by more than one member on the opposition side that my view would be prejudiced. However, if for no other reason than to try to clarify my own thinking, I propose to try to separate the various arguments in their generalities so that we can come to some basic conclusions on which to either agree or disagree.

I can do no better than to start with the argument of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas), who opened the debate from the standpoint of the opposition. I join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who complimented him. I think the Prime Minister described it as a thoughtful contribution, and I would add that I think it was generally objective. His basic objections, as I understood them, were that there was really no difference between this piece of legislation we have before us and the situation in which the petroleum and natural gas industry found itself in the past.
You will recall, sir, he then went on to say that we, as a government, had rejected or repudiated the Borden commission recommendations. There was, of course, some inconsistency there because one of his colleagues who followed him pointed out that the government had accepted some 23 of the recommendations and had rejected only 11. The point of his argument was that we had not employed-these are my own words-some of the tired, old Liberal ideas that had been left on the shelf for years. We had not put them into force as part of this energy bill. He quoted at length from Mr. John Davis who did a very fine job in the interests of the Gordon commission. He suggested that the government had not shown sufficient speed because they had sufficient material to establish an energy board, had they used the Gordon commission as a basis.
I wonder if the hon. member would reflect, first of all on the fact that this commission held its hearings some time ago, and certainly some time before the rather extreme changes which occurred in the economics of the industry. I believe that Mr. Davis might concede that he did not make as extensive a study or examination as Mr. Borden and his colleagues, and certainly his report would have needed updating. More important, the problems that he was asked by the commission to investigate were much broader than those objectives of the Borden commission, upon whose recommendations this energy bill is based. From one side of the house we have heard criticisms to the effect that the government has introduced more of the recommendations than it should, and from others we hear that it has not introduced enough.
Perhaps it is important to note that this government did not ignore the Borden royal commission recommendations as has been the habit for many years past of the previous governments, but rather it took the best from this report and rejected the balance. After all, that is their responsibility. I have, on more than one occasion, joined the critics in suggesting that Mr. Borden and his colleagues, first of all, did make a fine contribution to energy

resources in Canada by establishing a vast array of material for the development of a national oil and gas policy. I have also said that many of their recommendations, as I intend to show, have been adopted in this bill and will be beneficial, not only to the industry but to the consumer as well. As I have had occasion in the past to tell my friends in the oil industry, this commission was not established for any one particular group. It was established for the benefit of the public, regardless of whether they were developers of resources or just consumers.
The criticism which I have repeated many times in relation to the weakness in the Borden commission report-I think it is a human weakness-is that it fails above everything else in some of its recommendations to recognize that this is a business which involves great risks; great capital investment is required. I have been endeavouring to impress this on the house since I was first sent here. When one recalls that this industry spend a million and a half dollars a day in looking for these resources, it is quite obvious it is an undertaking that involves substantial capital and the risk factor is extreme.
I am going to leave this question and go on to the principal differences which the hon. member for Villeneuve says exist to the detriment of the industry. First of all, a board was established, and the Prime Minister dealt with that. I feel I certainly could not add to his remarks. A board was established, and that is something of which we should not lose sight.
Second, its advisory functions, I think, have not been given the weight or have not been put in the perspective in which they should have been put by many of the hon. members who have spoken. We hear to a considerable degree some of the comments with regard to the problems, first of all, in relation to the federal power commission of the United States and the problems of equating the amount of the reserves which are going to be required for Canadian consumption. These must be related also to the gas and oil that we anticipate to find, and the research that must be continually done in co-operation with the provinces. These are functions of an advisory nature which have never been carried out before and which will be carried out by this board. This is a second difference between what today we may look forward to and what has happened in the past.
A third rather distinct difference between what this bill proposes and what we have seen in the past is the simplification by which an applicant can appear before an agency of government to determine whether he has the right to construct a pipe line, and equally
National Energy Board important whether he has a right to export a hydrocarbon product. We know that under the old process it was necessary first of all to appear before the board of transport commissioners in order to obtain what we call a certificate of public convenience and this was given to the applicant who if successful received consent in the form of a certificate. He then had an additional problem of appealing through a second act for power to export. This gave him a licence, provided the minister conceded that this was acceptable. It was partly a discretionary power however.
I suggest that had this discretionary power been removed, had the present energy board been in force some three years ago and had the right of a public hearing been granted to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines in their initial application for an export permit, we would never have seen the situation by which this company eventually was asked to bring into the house an unprepared case and then drag out a hearing before the House of Commons in the pipe line debate. I am not suggesting that parliament should not have had that opportunity. But here we saw the minister of that government attempting to negotiate a contract which should have been the right of a public board, a body that would have had the opportunity to weigh the evidence, that would have been able to call witnesses and have them examined, and then to produce a finished recommendation on which the representatives of the people could then make a determination whether it was in the best interests of the people to grant a permit. It would have then been unnecessary to drag this long and extended application through the parliament of Canada. That is indeed a distinct difference between what we will see today and what has taken place in the past. But let me go on.
We have in this bill-and again repetition is unnecessary because the Prime Minister has dealt with the matter-provided for greater Canadian participation. I should like to say here that there is in some quarters in Canada a feeling that those involved in the petroleum industry of those outside it in western Canada are somewhat resentful of this suggestion. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, there are no more loyal Canadians, either in or outside of the petroleum industry, than there are in western Canada. We believe in the rights of Canadians no matter where those Canadians may live. We welcome Canadian participation as an inclusion in this bill.
Then we have, of course, the question of the regulation of tolls; and in this matter we see again the separation, in the past
performance of a government which saw
