National Energy Board no reason to regulate tolls in so far as they applied to gas. Indeed, this is another change in this bill which marks, so far as I have been able to count them, the fifth major change to date. I propose, Mr. Speaker, to make reference to others at a later point. But in discussing the change in the exercising or maintaining of a toll rate on gas lines, I should like to make what I hope will be construed by the hon. gentlemen on your left as an assessment which is done in all fairness of their arguments.
They have expressed considerable approval over Mr. Borden's recommendation of a fixed rate of return and asked whether something more stringent was still not necessary, something that was going to prevent the extreme profits of their Texas buccaneer from recurring.
I recall the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) dealing with the options which were granted to a group of executives of three companies in particular. At most they were a handful of men. I say very quickly that I do not justify extended options. I am not making a case for these gentlemen. They have been entitled to speak for themselves. However, what I say is this. Let us remember that when you fix a rate of return, when you apply any fixed formula controlling these returns, while it might have some influence on the Texas buccaneers, I suggest to them that it would also destroy completely the value of the shares, either present or future, held by many Canadians. Equally important, it would in my view eliminate the possibility of the construction of future pipe lines, certainly with private capital. Recognizing the difference in our ideologies, perhaps that matter is not of any real concern to them.
I suggest that we should remember that in one pipe line company alone-one which has been subjected to considerable publicity in this house-namely Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, there are 30,000 Canadians who would be affected as shareholders. They represent about 70 per cent of the share capital of that company. I suggest that when they invested their money as equity in this company they did so in the hope or the belief that it would not be interfered with by undue government regulation. It should be remembered that the principle of return based upon equity implies more rigorous control than we have ever experienced in Canadian industry. Certainly in peacetime, to regulate the return on equity we would have to decide whether the company could borrow money; if so, when and how much; and, finally of course, what rate of interest the bonds should pay and perhaps even who should buy them.

National Energy Board great bodies of ore, lead, zinc and iron which can be upgraded to a considerable degree and therefore utilized in a finished product within Canada. I suggest that here again is a matter to which the advisory board will certainly make a useful contribution.
On the question of any infringement on provincial rights, I was happy to hear the minister say in his statement that every effort had been made to avoid this. It was his view, I understood him to say, that there was no indication of any such infringement. Where there is any question of provincial rights it might be worthwhile, and I suggest it is worthwhile, if this problem might be referred to a body which I have often felt, while it performs a useful function, could make a more useful contribution to a board of this nature. I refer to the mines ministers' conference which, while it only meets annually, has a variety of committees which deal exactly with these and other subjects and could be used very effectively in an advisory capacity to the board as well. I point out that this consists of a group of men from industry and government in every province where there is any form of resources, and I suggest to the minister that he might usefully employ this body, to assist the energy board. I should like also to have the minister state clearly that there will be one hearing for an export permit after the order has been issued for a permit for convenience. I read the bill again at dinner time, and it did seem to me that there might be a need for clarification in this respect.
I come now to the last point I wish to make, and this concerns the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition when he dealt, first of all, with the problem of marketing oil in Canada, and with our domestic market. I thought his concern over the delay in the introduction of this bill was touching, because the concern which we have had in the province of Alberta has been with the delay which the Liberals in that province have shown in agreeing to the exportation of natural gas. It was refreshing to hear the hon. member for Villeneuve urge that immediate action should be taken. This is in contrast with the position taken by the leader in our province and it will be interesting to see what his comments will be in view of the hon. member's statement.
Then the Leader of the Opposition talks about the fact that there are no safeguards for Canadians. It is hardly necessary for me to dignify those comments by discussing them further. They have been dealt with. There was a complete lack of recognition of the fact that there is an important clause which deals with this point. He stated his view firmly


that there is no urgency whatsoever about granting authority to the governor in council to exercise the right to license imports and exports of oil. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) also dealt with this point.
I say, not in any heat of battle or debate, that I somehow get the feeling that hon. gentlemen opposite just do not understand the problems with which we are confronted. We have a marketing problem which is twofold. First, we export a volume of oil into what is known as district 5 of the United States and also into the mid-west of the United States. We import vast quantities- 290,000 barrels-of foreign crude into eastern Canada into the refining area of Montreal. Our problem is, one of markets for exports and, second, a problem of whether the imports of foreign crude coming into Canada are seriously reducing the markets which western Canadian oil has captured in eastern Canada.
Western Canadian oil men have never asked for any special advantage or consideration. What they do maintain is that when this oil comes in at firesale prices, at a dump rate, and the provisions of the anti-dumping act are not such that it can be prevented, then surely some form of regulation to protect the entire Canadian economy, not a segment of it, is essential.
It seems to me we are splitting hairs in determining how we are going to apply this principle of regulation in the bill. We can recall the Leader of the Opposition in Edmonton accepting the need of establishing oil markets in eastern Canada in the event that the restrictions by the United States on the entry of Canadian oil were not lifted. He must be equally honest with himself and recognize, while we are grateful that these restrictions have been lifted, and the indications are that we are going to benefit as Canadians as a result, that there is still no certainty that this will be a continuing benefit. If we are to continue to be able to market only about 45 per cent of our possible production, if dumped crude comes in from other parts of the world at six or nine cents a barrel compared with Canadian costs of $1 a barrel, is it not essential in the interests of the Canadian economy to have some type of legislation which can be employed immediately? I suggest that no one can appreciate this problem unless he recognizes the havoc that it can create in the industry.
As I have said many times, you cannot turn on a valve when you require oil or gas and then turn it off. You have to maintain a healthy industry. That is something which is entirely dependent on markets, and on continuous markets. If we found ourselves tomorrow in a situation where there

was a vast quantity of Russian crude on our doorstep, as we were a few short weeks ago with substantial quantities of crude from Venezuela, from Borneo and from the Middle East-crude that comes in at, say, 45 cents or 60 cents a barrel-below the price of Canadian oil, are hon. members going to tell me that the eastern Canadian consumer is going to benefit for more than just a few days? What about his line of supply? What if an emergency were to occur when these supplies of foreign crude were not available?
Is anyone going to argue that it is not essential that we should maintain a healthy economy based on a continuous supply of the product, and this is the basis on which this regulation can and will be implemented as I understand it. No one likes government regulation unless it is essential. The word "protection" has indeed become a dirty word. There are occasions, however, when one must recognize that the products we build or produce in Canada from our resources are essential in order to maintain economic unity, and without that economic equality how can we maintain national unity?
I should like to make one reference to the remarks of the Prime Minister. I have long been an advocate of the need for early action with regard to the export of our surplus natural gas based on the statistics which I have given to the house on many occasions in the past. This is not a question of trying to get rid of gas for quick profits. It is part of the argument I have just advanced in favour of the necessity of maintaining a continuous supply and a continuous market. I thank the Prime Minister for his statement that every consideration is going to be given to hearing the three applications currently before the board of transport commissioners, and that they will be transferred to the energy board. I accept his suggestion that they can be heard immediately following this debate and that the board would then be in a position, as I understand it, to hear these applications without any further delay.
I do not intend to go into Premier Manning's statements now, but in view of the Prime Minister's statement I feel we could ask for no more than has been offered. I think this is a satisfactory solution. I think it will provide the answer to the producers in western Canada to say, first of all, that the gas is going to be sold when it is surplus to the requirements of Canadians and that, on the other hand, in processing applications through the energy board the rights of the Canadian consumer will be adequately protected.
In these last moments I should like to say to my friends in the house that I have on
National Energy Board a number of occasions been overly sensitive to the suggestions that the petroleum industry and those of us in western Canada generally come from the land as it is so often described as "a fast buck". If you come from Calgary or that general area or have any connection with the petroleum industry one is regarded by many people as a cross between a procurer and a pickpocket, but I may assure hon. members that neither designation is true. While some may attempt to degrade the industry and its people in holding an exaggerated conception of wealth in their minds, let them remember some basic facts in relation to the industry. First of all the petroleum and natural gas industry is the number one mineral industry in Canada. Let them also be reminded that it was the greatest single factor in western Canada's postwar development. Let them remember, too, that when one single drilling rig moves into a community employing some twenty men it immediately contributes approximately $20,000 to the economic life of that area.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) for two reasons. In the first place I have a great personal respect for the hon. gentleman and second, I realize that he has a vast knowledge of the gas and oil industry

National Energy Board through his past association and no doubt because he comes from a part of the country where this industry is prominent. I do not necessarily always agree with what he says but I have a great deal of respect for the hon. gentleman.
The hon. member mentioned one point of considerable importance. If I heard him correctly he said that his only suspicion about this bill was that should hon. members of this group ever form the federal government the bill as it stands would give them much concern at that time. Perhaps I did not understand him correctly but I gathered from his remarks that this was the only reservation he had about this bill. I should like to know how hon. gentlemen opposite can have this suspicion when there is no proof? Why should they think that hon. members in this corner of the chamber would not suspect this bill when we in this corner have ample proof gathered over the years that there is need of more teeth in this legislation? If they are suspicious without any proof how can they expect hon. members in this group not to be suspicious when we have abundant proof before us based on the experience of the past?
I was most amused this afternoon at the example of the memory of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). How well that hon. gentleman's memory served him in taking him back to 1944 in talking about the great and terrible thing that the Saskatchewan government did at that time. This was also referred to by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). The Prime Minister's memory recall amazed me because his memory is so poor concerning what he himself said just two or three years ago. Interestingly enough, in referring to 1944 the Prime Minister did not substantiate his statements any more than did the hon. member for Edmonon West who when asked to specify yesterday said he could not remember the exact events but had given his impressions.
Perhaps most amusing of all was the smoke screen the Prime Minister tried to throw about the purchase of shares in certain companies by the provincial treasury of Saskatchewan. I am sure he intended to give the impression that the government of Saskatchewan is no different from the government of Ontario or any other province but there is one distinct difference. In the words of the Prime Minister himself it was the provincial treasury of the province of Saskatchewan that owned the shares; not the provincial treasurer, but the treasury. These

shares are still owned by the people of Saskatchewan and are not owned by the cabinet ministers-
Mr. Pallet!: What about the promoters of that transaction?

-nor the Tory friends of the Prime Minister, as we have seen in the province of Ontario. The Prime Minister did not mention that any of these shares were owned by the provincial president of the C.C.F. in Saskatchewan.
Mr. Pallet!: They are owned jointly by the government and the promoters.

speechtext:
Like we have seen shares owned by the president of the Conservative party in the province of Ontario. Indeed, he made no mention of the number of shares passed on to the leader of the Liberal opposition in the province of Saskatchewan like we have seen in Ontario. There is a marked difference between the practice in the province of Saskatchewan and that in the province of Ontario and other provinces.
Thus far in the debate we have heard no hon. member on the government side of the house point out how the Canadian public is going to receive any more protection under this bill than it has received in the past. Instead of citing my own opinions for a moment I should like to refer to an expression of opinion contained in an article by Mr. John Bird which appeared in the Toronto Star of Monday, May 25, 1959:
The public was shocked by the revelations of the Borden royal commission showing the perfectly legal "killings" made by the insiders in the Trans-Canada pipeline stock set-up. To control this sort of thing in future, the Borden report recommended relating pipeline tolls to the actual amount of equity capital in the venture.
Not only members of this group are concerned about this matter but many others who do not belong to this party are equally concerned. Another interesting point is contained in the final paragraph of this article:
And so, until the board is set up and we see how it functions, and particularly until we see what yardstick it uses for determining fair tolls and how carefully it examines the financial set-up of applicants for pipe lines, we shall have no way of knowing how far the public interest is to be safeguarded.
It is not too often that members of this group can turn to the Financial Post and find agreement with our comments and observations. But much to our surprise we find that in the May 23 edition of the Financial Post the biggest part of one page is devoted to the very problem under discussion at the present time in an article by Michael Barkway. I have not studied the material there thoroughly but I find that there are at least 15 places where concern is

shown in the Financial Post article along the same lines expressed by members of this group. I think that some of these observations could very well be put on the record. The headline reads as follows: "How Ottawa Plans to Control Pipe Lines; National Energy Bill Would Regulate Rates, Tolls and Export Prices, But Standards Are Not Laid Down." The article goes on to point out in many places the views expressed by the members of this group and, indeed, expressed by myself when I spoke on this matter yesterday. The article points out that in clause after clause control is left firmly in the hands of the cabinet. The new board that is to be set up is not being given the jurisdiction that it should have. The article states:
Wide powers to regulate oil and gas pipe lines and export of electrical energy are conferred on the Cabinet-
Farther down it goes on to say that all gas and oil pipe lines which come under federal jurisdiction will require a certificate of convenience and necessity "but its issue will be subject to cabinet approval". It goes on to point out that international power lines for the export of electric power will be subject to the same cabinet approval and that the export and import of gas and export of power will be subject to regulations to be issued by the cabinet itself. We go down farther and we see there is a reference to "general cabinet regulations, within the terms of which the national energy board may grant licences". In another place it is pointed out that the decision of the board will depend on government approval in two different ways. In another place it says:
But the certificate will not be issued without government approval.
Then the article goes on to say:
The wording of the bill says: "The board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate'-
And further:
But very wide discretion is left to the members of the national energy board to find a basis for setting a rate of return. subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very little can be added in the closing hour or so of the debate on the bill to set up a national energy board. I should like to try to kill once and for all one red herring that has been dragged in by the official opposition. It was brought in tonight by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) when he referred to the 15 per cent trade diversion and the 15 per cent reduction in oil imports by the United States. In the early months of 1957 I happened to be a senior engineer with perhaps the largest pipe line contracting firm in the world. At that time the official journal of the oil industry in the United States was full of the submissions which were being made to Washington, particularly by the independent producers in Texas, asking for mandatory restrictions on oil imports, and the figure mentioned in issue after issue of this journal was 15 per cent.
The reason they were asking for this restriction was that it was claimed the independent producers in Texas were operating at about one-half maximum efficient capacity because the majority of the refining capacity was in the hands of the majors and the independents could not sell as much as they wished to the majors. The majors had enough of their own oil coming in from offshore concessions to satisfy a large part of their requirements. This 15 per cent business is about the most arrant piece of nonsense that I have heard in this house in the length of time I have been here. I am seeking very carefully for words which will not be called unparliamentary in order to describe the antics that have been gone through in this regard.
In so far as the possible control of oil imports is concerned, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) has made a very able speech pointing out the necessity for it. I should like to add a few remarks covering a few points which he did not mention. It is not generally known, but the approximate cost of bringing a barrel of oil to the surface is half a cent per barrel in the Near East; 65 cents in Venezuela; 90 cents in Canada and $1.20 in the United States. The reason for this, of course, is that a well in the Near East will be producing 10,000, 20,000 or 30,000 barrels per day, whereas in Canada a well will produce 20 to 30 barrels per day on the average. Our wells are operating at about half the capacity the wells in Texas were

operating when the Texas producers demanded that a state of emergency be declared and that oil imports be limited because production in Texas had dropped so low. Our western producers were in, and are in, a far worse position than the Texas producers ever were.
We have heard something about this point of commercial preference. It sounds complicated, but it is very simple. It simply means this, that the major oil companies are world wide organizations, fully integrated and owning producing fields in Venezuela, in Sumatra and in the Near East. When they import this oil they are buying it from themselves, and they can set whatever price they wish on it. They also have the advantage when they use it in their refineries of using 100 per cent of their own oil. When they use western Canadian oil, because all wells are on a pro rata system, the independents and the majors alike pump into the gathering systems according to the number of wells that they have in production and on the basis of the quota that they have been allotted by the provincial board governing that matter. Therefore, when they use Canadian oil they get only that percentage of their own oil that this percentage bears to the total production of all wells in western Canada. It is therefore much more advantageous for a company to use its own offshore oil.
It is also advantageous from the point of view that oil in Canada is safe but oil in these other areas I have mentioned is unsafe because of unstable political conditions. Mr. Harold Rea, president of the Canadian Oil Company, speaking to the Harvard club in Tulsa, Oklahoma, had this to say, and I quote:
"Large U.S. companies with substantial oil reserves in Canada, and facilities to market that oil in the U.S., should do so."
Companies should not tie up great tracts of exploratory land in Canada and put their reserves of Canadian crude in "mothballs" while, at the same time, eastern Canada must import large quantities of foreign-produced oil. Mr. Rea stated.
At the conclusion of the Borden commission hearings the oil companies voluntarily agreed that they would use more western oil in the Toronto refining area, and they would back up oil which was being refined in the Montreal area to give a greater marketing area to the refined products from Toronto. This was to increase the use of Canadian crude. They also agreed that in the oil deficiency areas of the United States, that is district No. 5 comprising Washington, Oregon and the northern part of California, those refineries which were connected by pipe line through Trans-Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company to sources of Canadian crude, would be allowed a greater degree of freedom in the amount of oil that

they purchased. In fact, they were not originally on a quota basis so far as the United States government was concerned, but so far as the operation of the oil companies is concerned they are on a quota which is based on how best they can use their reserves to make the most profits for themselves. This operation dictated the use of offshore oil.
Now, when we talk about the importation of 290,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan oil into the Montreal market, we really mean 290,000 barrels per day of United States oil because that oil comes from companies owned and controlled in the United States. It is only fair and reasonable that we should be able to use this major import as bargaining lever with the United States to promote the flow of our oil into our natural market, that is the oil deficiency area of district No. 5 in the Pacific northwest and the oil deficiency areas in the midwest United States. It is for that reason I believe the mandatory controls have been lifted. As the hon. member for Ottawa West did point out, there was an article in this morning's Gazette by Mr. Meyer, the financial editor, pointing out that even the elimination of this mandatory control still leaves the ceiling section in the regulations which prohibits the importation of Canadian oil in excess of the quota arrangements we had been given previously. I am not sure whether or not Mr. Meyer has properly interpreted the regulations, but if he has we can only gain back the ground we have lost, and that will not be satisfactory. It is for this reason that in this bill the government is being given the power to use this importation of 290,000 barrels of oil per day as a bargaining lever. If it does not work out that way, then there is always the alternative of supplying our own oil to this major Canadian market.
So far as the companies are concerned, as I have tried to point out, through commercial preference and the integrated operation between the producing fields and the refining and distributing set-up, the world wide company can pretty well set what price it wants to set on its own oil; but that price means nothing.
But what does mean something, incidentally, is that the underdeveloped countries are demanding a greater and greater share in the profits from the mining of their oil. Where Anglo-Iranian could get by with a 25-75 split, Aramco today are signing contracts on a 60-40 basis, with 60 per cent for Saudi Arabia. Hence the costs of this so-called cheap oil are going up. There is still that major factor of the political instability of these countries and the necessity for the international oil companies to plow back into those countries revenues in the form of royalties
National Energy Board in order to maintain the government which they have. This is their problem; it is not ours.
Reverting to the question of natural gas, there is one point on which I will disagree with my friend the hon. member for Calgary South, namely with regard to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company. Trans-Canada today is a good company controlled by Canadians. As the hon. member pointed out, some 80,000 Canadians have shares in it. I have talked to the president. The company has almost 100 per cent Canadian personnel now and in every respect it is a good company. It is a good company for the people of Canada and a good company for its own employees. When that company was set up I believe the names which would appear as the largest shareholders start off with Mr. Murchison and run through the gamut of the so-called Texas buccaneers. These people sold out. They sold out their cheap stock at a fairly good price to people like Home Oil and others. Canadians paid good prices for this stock which these people obtained as a gift through the policies of the previous administration.
I should like to make particular reference to gas as it affects Vancouver. I will quote from an editorial of Thursday, February 20, 1958 which appeared in the Vancouver Province. It has to do with the sale price of gas to the Pacific Northwest Pipe Line Company and to the British Columbia Electric Company. This editorial is headed "Bilked on our own gas" and it reads in part as follows:
The Borden commission in its Calgary hearings has already laid bare, and in fact openly suggests, that the Canadian public is being bilked in the promotion and sale of its natural gas.
The situation in British Columbia is presently under examination. Distributors in the United States are buying our natural gas at the border for 22 cents a thousand cubic feet. Canadian distributors pay 32 cents a thousand cubic feet.
The Westcoast Transmission Co. Ltd. has made a 20-year contract to deliver natural gas from northern B.C. and Alberta to the Pacific Northwest-
That is Pacific Northwest Pipe Line Corporation.
-for 22 cents.
The chairman of the commission, Henry Borden, has been moved to comment in open hearings that this export of Canadian gas is "unprofitable."
The editorial goes on to say this:
Commission counsel has shown that it costs 24 cents to deliver the gas to the border. He has also suggested that any profit on this kind of operations must come out of the Canadian consumer.
The editorial is broken into two parts. In the second half it goes on to state as follows:
The gas-price situation being examined by the Borden commission could-and should-brew up into a first-class political scandal.
During their years in power the Liberals insisted repeatedly that their policy was to protect the interests of Canadian gas consumers.

National Energy Board
On March 13, 1953, the then minister of trade and commerce, Mr. C. D. Howe, declared proudly that while the Conservatives were talking of a "Canada first" gas policy, the Liberals went farther: their policy was "Canada always."
On April 15, 1953, announcing the granting of a 22-year permit to Westcoast Transmission, Mr. Howe said flatly in Commons that "the interests of British Columbia customers will be protected."
On June 4, 1956, the then minister of finance, Mr. Walter Harris, quoted regulation No. 9 of the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, and said:
"This means, Mr. Speaker, that when a licence is granted for the export of gas out of Canada-and that licence has not yet been granted-it is going to be subject to these regulations, and these regulations will be enforced by the government of Canada to see that the export of gas is not at a price lower than the price for gas supplied in Canada."
What is regulation No. 9? It was quoted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon.
The said regulation No. 9, drafted by the Liberal government, reads: "The price charged by a licencee for power or gas exported by him shall not be lower than the price at which power or gas, respectively, is supplied by him or his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumpton in Canada."
The loophole is the phrase "in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale."
The Borden report went into great detail on this matter. I should like to say that this condition came about through no fault of Westcoast Transmission. The promoters of Westcoast Transmission spent great sums of money and had brought it to the point where it had no future because they were denied the right to export gas to the United States. It looked like a lost cause. When they were offered this arrangement from Pacific Northwest they were obliged to accept or see the whole project fall through completely. I have been up around Dawson Creek where the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) lives and Fort St. John and Taylor. He can tell you better than I of the industrial activity and the vitality that has come to that country through the building of this gas pipe line. But that is not to say that we should not expect to get these benefits in the future without sacrificing any part of our birthright.
The Pacific Northwest Company drove a hard bargain with Westcoast Transmission. I now quote from page 17 of the Borden report which states as follows:
In December, 1954, as a part of the consideration for executing the gas purchase contract with Westcoast, Pacific Northwest demanded a 50 per cent share interest in Westcoast but accepted an option, dated December 11, 1954, in favour of one K.S. Adams, to purchase common shares equivalent to 25 per cent of the common shares of Westcoast outstanding after its public financing and at the price at which shares would be offered to the public.
The result of this was that Pacific Northwest acquired 1,127,750 of its common shares

at the price of $5 per share. Those shares were $16 on the market right after the public offering. So we have this United States company paying far less for their gas than does the Canadian distributor which incidentally is taking off at the same take-off point as the United States company. The United States company to boot has obtained 25 per cent of the stock of the transmission line. Finally, any profits made by the transmission company will be made on the sale of gas to Canadians and the United States company will get 25 per cent of that amount also. This is the sort of thing that is meant in this bill in clause 44 where reference is made to the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line and the question of any public interest which may be involved.
It seems that although the Borden commission talk about sanctity of contracts I see no sanctity in the contract with Pacific Northwest. I believe one of the first acts of the energy board should be to review this matter to the end that the gas sold in the United States or any exported gas is not sold at any more favourable price than it is offered to Canadian consumers.
The final point I would like to make is in regard to Canadian participation in these companies and the fact that the bill itself states that the commission shall see to it that financing is carried on in such a way that Canadians participate. I do not think there should be an offering of any pipe line shares other than in Canada. I think the method used to finance the Alberta trunk gas lines is an excellent form to follow, except of course in that case it was restricted to the residents of Alberta alone. I am convinced that the people of Canada do have the courage to invest in risk enterprises like this, because a pipe line is a tremendous risk. It is a gamble and if it fails then there are literally millions of dollars lost, because with a pipe line there is no halfway measure. But I believe that Canadians do wish to participate and wish to have the right to subscribe at the initial offering of stock in these companies, and this bill will see that Canadians will have that right.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what all the talk is from the opposition benches? We have heard more twaddle, more vagueness, more lack of understanding of this whole question from the opposition benches than anything I can recall having listened to in the house before. The hon. member for

Timmins (Mr. Martin), an admirable fellow in many ways, talked about the cabinet taking the responsibility and not the energy board. Of course the cabinet has the responsibility. The energy board does not have to report to the Canadian people, but the cabinet does, and through their elected representatives the Canadian people will have control and will be able to say whether they do or do not agree with the way this board is working. It seems to me that that is the only possible way to make this work. Undoubtedly there will be a period of trial and error. There will have to be minor modifications, but the bill has been so framed that not only is there freedom for the board to work but there is also the saving grace of cabinet approval. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we get on to the details of the bill as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak for a few moments tonight on the export of gas and what I think should be done in connection with the Canadian consumer.
With the discovery of vast quantities of natural gas and the subsequent construction of pipe lines throughout Canada and the United States, natural gas is fast replacing many other types of fuel in communities which are fortunate enough to have this modern convenient type of fuel. In the years to come any community that is not serviced by this modern convenience when the pipe line is in construction will be seriously handicapped in its development. Western Canada has been blessed with an abundance of natural gas and large quantities of this fuel to export to areas which are less fortunate. We would definitely urge the exporting of gas in order that the economy of Canada may benefit.
First, Mr. Speaker, we would like to recommend return on capital invested in the gas and oil industries. We feel that the investors are entitled to a return on their investments. Second, the creation of employment for Canadians in the construction of gas lines and gathering systems, scrubbing plants and also the development of by-products from the gas itself. Third, the creation of permanent employment for Canadians in the maintenance and operation of these installations. Fourth, giving the gas companies encouragement to continue further explorations for new fields, and I believe many of these could be found in southeastern British Columbia.
However, Mr. Speaker, before permits for the export of natural gas are granted by the department provision should be made to supply Canadian communities within reasonable range of the main transmission line which
National Energy Board desire to be serviced with adequate gas supplies at a reasonable rate. There will very shortly be an application or applications presented to the energy board by the Alberta and Southern Gas Company Limited and the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited to export approximately three trillion cubic feet of natural gas from Alberta to the Pacific northwestern states. The proposed pipe line will transport gas from the Alberta border at the Crowsnest pass to the international boundary at Kingsgate, British Columbia, travelling through that part of British Columbia more commonly known as the east Kootenay.
In the east Kootenay there are six organized municipalities, namely the cities of Fernie, Cranbrook, Kimberley, two small villages of Marysville and Chapman Camp, and the rapidly expanding district of Creston. These communities are very desirous of being served with natural gas and the only possible source of this fuel for these communities will be this pipe line solely designed for export purposes. We feel that if these communities are serviced at the time of construction we will have an added incentive for industry to come into our area.
Mr. Speaker, due to the location of this pipe line-incidentally I have been over part of the present survey-it is not economically possible to serve the above mentioned communities, with the exception of Fernie, by the main pipe line. Therefore we are going to need branch lines taken off the main service lines. The cost of transportation of gas from the pipe line as presently proposed to the boundaries of these municipalities desiring the service would make the cost of the gas very high to the consumer. However, if the export pipe line company were to include the cost of these distribution lines to the various communities which I have named, bringing them to the boundaries of their municipalities, in the over-all cost of the pipe line, so that the entire volume of gas carried would bear its share of the cost, the increase per million cubic feet would be very nominal.
We have watched with consternation the establishment of rates for natural gas on the previously constructed pipe lines. The fact that Canadian utilities, for example Inland Natural Gas Company Limited and the British Columbia Electric Company, pay more for gas than the United States utility companies, for example Northwest Utility Company, is a situation which does not meet with approval in Canada, and in British Columbia in particular. In the opinion of some of the experts Canadians are subsidizing United States gas. This should not be the case. It would be more reasonable to expect the reverse. In the present application the maximum Canadian

National Energy Board consumption would be approximately 2 per cent of the gas carried and it is not unreasonable that 98 per cent should subsidize the 2 per cent for the privilege of export. This is a matter which is very important to the Canadian communities concerned.
In our area we have an abundance of raw materials. We have practically all the raw materials that are required for the manufacture of a great number of articles. We should like to be in such a position that when the gas lines are brought to the edge of the municipalities we could apply for it and derive the benefits of this gas without the necessity of making formal application to various boards. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) has mentioned the difference in the Vancouver rate, and pointed out that Vancouver is paying approximately 50 per cent more for gas than the people across the line.
I wish to bring three points to the attention of the house. I think when this gas line is constructed it should supply natural gas to the cities of Cranbrook and Kimberley and to the villages of Marysville, Chapman Camp and Creston; that the companies should sell the gas to these communities at the same cost as sold at the international boundary, and that they should deliver the gas to the boundaries of the municipalities concerned.

This measure is concerned with the government's

policy on natural energy. I did not know it had anything to do with a cement factory;
I did not know it had anything to do with a steel factory. But the Prime Minister, in saying that public ownership is not the best type of ownership, takes us out to Saskatchewan and talks about a cement factory and talks about pipe lines.

First, the immediate agreement of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to reorganize as a company under effective Canadian ownership and control and

National Energy Board to undertake construction without a grant of public money, in accordance with the assurances upon which its charter was granted by parliament; or-
There is no indication now that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited is to reorganize as a company under effective Canadian ownership. In introducing the legislation the minister said that as far as the government was concerned it would welcome Canadian and foreign capital. All that means in the context of this legislation is that the government is prepared to have pipe lines built and controlled by outside capital. It can mean nothing else because there is no control based on Canadian capital and no control to prevent foreign capital from controlling this industry.
I continue with the words of the motion of Mr. Drew:
Second, failing such agreement, the immediate consideration of other proposals submitted by any other persons or companies for the immediate financing and construction of the pipe line under effective Canadian ownership and control and without a grant of public money; or
Third, enlarge the powers of the crown corporation so that the entire pipe line may be constructed immediately under public ownership.
The Conservatives in 1956 were prepared to accept public ownership as an alternative policy to that being followed by the government of the day. Today they not only reject public ownership but they reject any effective control that would guarantee that this industry and other energy in Canada be developed by Canadians and by Canadian capital.
This government has made a complete about face. It has turned its back on its own statement and its own record. Not only is it prepared to allow this industry to fall more completely into the hands of outside persons and outside capital but it is not prepared as outlined in this bill to give the
energy board any effective power to deal with the development and control of energy in Canada.
